an-examination-of-phrenology-in-two-lect: An Examination of Phrenology, 1838. The two lectures. This book preserves that examination. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
anderson-constitutions-1738:
James Anderson, a Scottish minister in London, rewrote his Constitutions of the Free-Masons for this second edition of 1738. The first edition of 1723 had founded modern Freemasonry on paper. The New Book of Constitutions recasts that work substantially, with a fuller legendary history and revised charges and regulations for the Grand Lodge.

Anderson's history carries Masonry from Adam through the builders of Scripture and the kings of Britain. His charges set the Craft's famous rules on God, government, and conduct. The library holds the 1723 first edition; this 1738 text shows the founding document growing. Every later Masonic constitution descends from Anderson's pages in one of their two forms.
arxiv-2512-00238:
Spinors describe particles with spin, and their duals are a subtle part of quantum field theory. Cavalcanti and Hoff da Silva present a unified approach to spinor duals in 2025, built on Clifford algebras and related symmetry groups. Recent work has revealed several distinct algebraic formulations of generalized Dirac duals.

Different dual constructions can lead to different physical models, so a unified view helps theorists compare them safely. The authors locate these formulations inside the structure of a complex Clifford algebra. The work is mathematical physics, aimed at readers who build field theory models from algebraic first principles. Clifford algebras unify rotations and reflections, which is why spinor theory leans on them.
arxiv-2512-00538:
Large optimization problems often exist at several resolutions at once, from coarse grids to fine ones. Robert Baraldi, Michael Hintermüller, and Qi Wang present a multilevel proximal trust-region method for nonsmooth optimization in 2025, with applications. Multilevel methods exploit that hierarchy to converge faster.

Combining coarse and fine information has proved highly effective for partial differential equations and related problems. Trust-region methods control step sizes, while proximal terms handle nonsmooth structure that gradients alone cannot. The method targets science and engineering problems whose scale defeats single-level algorithms. Nonsmooth problems include contact and friction, where gradients jump or fail to exist. Proximal methods are the standard toolkit for exactly that structure.
arxiv-2512-00738:
Paul Oamen, Robert Wesley, and Pius Onobhayedo wrote a 2025 paper on loyalty programs in the age of smart commerce. Reward schemes have grown from copper tokens to complex digital systems. Yet most programs stay closed, with one brand controlling the points, rules, and rewards.

Coalition programs let points work across brands, which should help everyone. Still, the authors note that many such coalitions fail within ten years, despite the network gains theory predicts. Their paper asks how rewards should be orchestrated so partners share value fairly. The lessons matter for retailers building joint programs that last.
arxiv-2512-00838:
Md Muzakkir Quamar, Ali Nasir, and Sami ELFerik present a planning framework for drones in a 2025 paper. Unmanned aerial vehicles must plan missions in complex, uncertain settings, from shifting weather to failing parts. Good plans are often computed with Markov decision processes, which weigh actions, chances, and rewards together.

Those processes grow too large to solve directly as missions scale up. The team's two-stage decomposition breaks the big problem into smaller pieces that can be solved and recombined. The framework is built to be scalable and fault-tolerant. Faster, sturdier planning would let drone fleets take on bigger jobs.
arxiv-2512-01038:
Hetvi Shastri and four coauthors present FMTK in a 2025 paper on time series tools. Foundation models adapt to new tasks with little or no extra training, and time-series foundation models do the same for data that unfolds over time. They have shown strong results on classification, regression, and filling missing values.

FMTK is a modular toolkit for building composable pipelines from such models. Users can mix and match stages instead of rebuilding a whole system for each job. Modularity matters because time series work spans forecasting, monitoring, and health signals, each with its own steps. A shared toolkit lowers the cost of trying foundation models on real problems.
arxiv-2512-01138:
Search tasks that always have an answer sit at the heart of this study. Some can be solved fast by a chance-based method. The work starts a close study of that class of tasks. It groups tasks that a fast random method can always solve.

Examples include finding a prime in a fixed range. They also include tasks that test claims about circuit limits. The study maps what sits in the class and how its parts link. A clear map helps show which hard search tasks may yield to fast random methods and which may not.
arxiv-2512-01338:
Sanjeeda Sultana, Chayan Ranjit, and Surajit Chattopadhyay rebuild a dark energy model. The model mixes a Chaplygin gas with holographic dark energy in the Barrow frame. That frame tweaks how entropy works at the edge of space. Such models try to explain why the cosmos grows faster over time.

The team checks if the rebuilt model obeys the broad law of thermodynamics. They also bound its values with fresh data from space probes. A model that passes both checks stays in the race. One that fails helps rule out paths for dark energy theory.
arxiv-2512-01538:
Marco Romanelli, Gabriel Gil, and Stefano Corni quantize light modes of metal nanoparticles. Tiny metal bits can trap light as plasmons. Their shape can be any form, not just spheres. The metal's response shifts with light tone in ways set by real data.

Their method handles odd shapes with that real response built in. Quantized modes let scholars compute quantum effects of plasmons. Those effects matter for sensors and light tools at tiny scales. A general method frees the work from shape-by-shape hand math. Experimental dielectric data anchor the modes, so predicted resonances can be checked against measured spectra for real metals, not ideal ones.
arxiv-2512-01638:
Zvirzdin searches for ultra-high-energy photons with the Telescope Array. Such photons can test astrophysics models and new physics. The array's surface detector has run for many years. Its data holds a vast set of air shower events.

A neural network sorts showers by their likely source particle. Photon showers differ in shape from proton showers. The sort yields updated caps on the diffuse photon flux. Tight caps rule out models that would flood the sky with such photons. They also bound exotic ideas about dark matter decay. Fourteen years of data give the caps weight, since rare photon showers need huge exposure before a null result means anything at all.
arxiv-2512-01738:
Pedro Curvo, Jan-Willem van de Meent, and Maksim Zhdanov scale neural solvers to industrial physics. Large simulations must capture fine local acts and long-range links at once. Millions of spatial elements make both hard. Attention over all elements is too costly.

Their Multi-Scale Patch Transformer splits the task. Local attention works inside patches of elements. Global attention works on coarse patch summaries. That split keeps fine detail without full cost. Industrial users could run larger, truer physics models with learned speed. Patch summaries carry the far field cheaply, much as multigrid solvers do, which is why the design scales near linearly in tests.
arxiv-2512-02138:
Networks of machines, from drone swarms to power grids, are often built from parts that are individually easy to control. Fengjun Yang, Jake Welde, and Nikolai Matni study in 2025 what happens when those parts are coupled: the whole network can lose the flatness property that made each part simple.

Differential flatness lets engineers plan motion and design controllers with unusual ease for a single subsystem. The authors seek distributed control that survives coupling designed to preserve flatness across the network. Their results matter wherever many nonlinear units must cooperate, because a control scheme that only works in isolation fails exactly when the system becomes interesting.
arxiv-2512-02238:
Roger Penrose held that time's arrow is writ in the shape of space. As things form, one kind of curve in that shape, Weyl curvature, should come to dwarf the other kind. Four authors led by R. A. Sussman take a fresh look in 2025 at what they call a long-held false take on this Weyl claim.

A claimed counter-case by Bonnor used exact math for hot spheres that fall inward in a Vaidya setting. The team rechecks that case and what the claim in fact says. The stakes are high. The claim ties the smooth start of the cosmos to the rule that disorder must grow.
arxiv-2512-02538:
Nathanaël Berestycki gives a concise tour of the hidden sound spectrum of Liouville quantum gravity. That theory describes a random, fractal like geometry meant to model quantum space. On it runs Liouville Brownian motion, the natural random walk for such a strange landscape.

Berestycki lays out how the motion's eigenvalues and eigenfunctions are built, forming the spectrum of the geometry. He also summarizes a recently proved Weyl law, which counts those tones at high frequency. Work in progress on the heat trace is reported too, linking the spectrum to how heat would spread on quantum geometry. The talk also serves as a map for those who want to learn this young field from the ground up.
arxiv-2512-02738:
Joel Nyholm, Wojciech Mostowski, and Christoph Reichenbach profile energy use down to single lines of code. Energy demand grows from phones to huge data centers, and developers need detail to fix waste. Older profilers blame whole programs or single functions, which is too coarse to act on.

Their probabilistic profiler targets statically typed JVM based languages, including Java. It estimates energy per source statement, with uncertainty stated openly. Line level feedback could help teams cut the energy cost of common software, a growing share of global electricity use. Line by line costs show staff the exact line that eats the watts, not just the app as a whole blob.
arxiv-2512-02838:
Ridha Horchani drafts an experiment to tell two explanations of the classical world apart. Quantum theory allows macroscopic superpositions, yet daily life never shows them. Either the environment steadily erases them, a process called decoherence, or the wave function collapses on its own.

Both stories predict similar everyday behavior, so telling them apart takes care. Horchani's blueprint lays out how a real experiment could distinguish the two mechanisms. A working test would strike at one of the deepest open questions in physics, the border between quantum and classical. Two tales that match on all past tests can still split on the next one, and this plan names that next test in full.
arxiv-2512-02938:
Maksymilian Kuna and seven co-authors show that a weak magnetic field brightens valley control in a tungsten diselenide sheet. The monolayer was grown by molecular beam epitaxy on hexagonal boron nitride. Valley polarization measures which of two electron valleys the light emission favors.

Circularly polarized photoluminescence measurements track that balance as a field is applied. A field on the order of a tenth of a tesla already enhances the polarization, the authors report. Easy valley control in grown monolayers supports valleytronic devices, which store information in electron valleys. Weak fields are cheap to add and safe for the flake. So a boost at low field is worth more than one that needs a huge rig to run.
arxiv-2512-03038:
Giulio Fabbian and six co-authors remeasure a faint distortion in the cosmic microwave background's spectrum. The y type distortion records the pressure of hot gas trapped in galaxy groups and clusters. Archival data from the FIRAS instrument still holds untapped signal for this measurement.

With improved cleaning of astrophysical foregrounds, the team extracts a new mean distortion value. The result carries implications for feedback models in galaxy formation and for cosmic shear measurements. Old satellite data, reanalyzed well, can still sharpen how we model gas in the universe. Old tapes with new eyes is a cheap trick with real yield. This yield is a mark that gas rich clumps must match in their own tales of growth.
arxiv-2512-03238:
Synthetic data can train AI without exposing real records. Natalia Ponomareva and a large team offer a practical guide in this 2025 work. They focus on making such data with differential privacy, which bounds what can be learned about any one person.

Good data are vital for AI, yet fresh human data are getting scarce. The guide, called how to DP-fy your data, walks through the process step by step. Clear guidance helps firms share and use data safely. It also helps meet privacy rules while still training useful models. Step-by-step guidance lowers the barrier for teams with data but no privacy experts.
arxiv-2512-03438:
Rewarding only final answers can starve agent training. Reuben Tan and a large team address that in this 2025 work on multimodal reinforcement learning. Agentic models are capable, yet sparse outcome rewards dominate their training.

Rewards computed from reasoning tokens give finer guidance during learning. The authors add an agentic verifier to supply those richer rewards. Finer feedback can teach agents to plan and check their work. That may raise reliability in tasks that mix text, images, and tools. Reasoning-token rewards teach process, not just outcomes, which may curb lucky but flawed answers in multimodal agent training.
arxiv-2601-06638:
J. J. Segura finds an exact rule for how grain sizes change as they break, in 2026. Breakage rules track how the spread of grain sizes shifts over time. Bits from each break are shared out to new, smaller sizes.

From a self-similar class of breaks, he derives an exact move rule. The rule works on the log of size, for the share of mass at each size. It takes the form of a pure-jump master rule, as he shows. Mass moves in jumps in log size, not in a smooth drift at all. From it he draws drift and spread limits for large scales. The frame also helps infer the size spread from test data. Those who model mills get exact form first, not rough fits.
arxiv-2601-06938:
Heng Xu and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with forgetting similar samples. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Machine unlearning, a process enabling pre-trained models to remove the influence of specific training samples, has attracted significant attention in recent years. Although extensive research has focused on developing efficient machine unlearning strategies.

We argue that these methods mainly aim at removing samples rather than removing samples’ influence on the model. Thus overlooking the fundamental definition of machine unlearning. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07038:
Emma Rafkin and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers task arithmetic with support languages for Low-Resource ASR. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. The development of resource-constrained approaches to automatic speech recognition (ASR) is of great interest due to its broad applicability to many low-resource languages.

For which there is scant usable data. Existing approaches to many low-resource natural language processing tasks leverage additional data from higher-resource languages that are closely related to a target low-resource language. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07238:
Hanbin Wang and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers group pattern selection optimization. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Large reasoning models (LRMs) exhibit diverse high-level reasoning patterns (e.g., direct solution, reflection-and-verification, and exploring multiple solutions). Yet prevailing training recipes implicitly bias models toward a limited set of dominant patterns.

Through a systematic analysis, we identify substantial accuracy variance across these patterns on mathematics and science benchmarks. Revealing that a model’s default reasoning pattern is often sub-optimal for a given problem. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07338:
An arXiv preprint from 2026 covers beyond literal mapping. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced Machine Translation (MT), applying them to linguistically complex domains—such as Social Network Services, literature etc.

In these scenarios, translations often require handling non-literal expressions, leading to the inaccuracy of MT metrics. To systematically investigate the reliability of MT metrics, we first curate a meta-evaluation dataset focused on non-literal translations, namely MENT . The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07638:
Isaiah Onando Mulang' and colleagues build a benchmark for learning from business tables with meaning attached. SALT-KG extends the earlier SALT benchmark for relational prediction. The new version links multi-table transaction data to a structured knowledge graph of operational business knowledge. That graph records field-level descriptions, relations between fields, and business object types. Their 2026 preprint defines the resource.

Most table benchmarks give models numbers without the business context behind them. Semantics-aware learning tests whether models can use that context to predict better. Enterprise data is exactly where such context exists but is rarely shared. A public benchmark lets teams compare methods fairly. The paper targets machine learning scholars who work with relational and enterprise data.
arxiv-2601-08238: Jia-Wei Ying and co-authors design quantum secure direct communication that ignores reference frame drift. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that current protocols check photon error rates in two bases. Those checks assume the two parties first calibrate a shared reference frame. In mobile settings, keeping that calibration continuous and accurate is hard. A reference-frame-independent protocol removes the prerequisite entirely. The work targets secure links on moving platforms, where alignment shifts constantly. Quantum direct communication sends the message itself, so frame freedom could widen its practical reach.
arxiv-2601-08938:
Michael Weber, Barbara Ercolano, and Giovanni Picogna ask if star light alone can carve gaps in young disks of gas and dust. Such disks form round new stars, and planets grow in them. Light from the star can boil gas off the disk face. That boil off is called photoevaporation. Some claim it can open a clean gap, as a planet can.

The team runs 2D sims that tie disk growth to the boil off flow. They find a catch. Once a dip forms, the boil off rate there drops fast. That drop stops the gap from deep growth. A reader in planet birth work gets a bound on what star light can do alone.
arxiv-2601-09138:
Sahas Kamat and five co-authors report a vast zone of shakes in a heavy superconductor named UTe2. A superconductor bears charge with no loss under a set heat. In most such stuffs, shakes near the shift heat span a thin band. Past that band, a plain mean law holds well. In UTe2 the shake band is as wide as the shift heat itself.

That width is the large known for a stuff of this type, the team says. It hints that pairs of charge bits form across bands, not in one band. Such cross band pairs would break the plain law in just this way. A reader in new stuffs gets a case that may force a fresh take on how pairs form.
arxiv-2601-09238:
Jackie Alex and Justin Petter grow fake flaw shots of power sub station meters from a few real ones. Such meters watch grid health. Cracks and flaws on them must be caught. Marked real shots of flaws are rare, so a spot tool starves for train data. A grow tool can fill that gap, if its fakes look true and can be set by type.

Their frame adds fact codes and a hyper net guide to a spread based grow tool. The guide steers flaw type, place, and size from few cases. A reader in grid work gets train shots for a rare flaw hunt, with a hand on what each fake shows.
arxiv-2601-09338:
Yao Sun and four co-authors chart all study work on OpenStreetMap from its start to 2024. OSM is a free world map built by vol hands. It grew from a bold side task to a base for work in maps, towns, aid, and nets. The team runs a count and theme scan of that study set to see who built it, and what they asked.

They track how themes shifted as the map grew. Early work asked if vol maps could be true. Late work uses the map as firm data for hard asks. A reader in map work gets a guide to a vast field, and a view of where it may go next.
arxiv-2601-09638:
A. Rigoulet, S. Nanos, I. K. Kominis, and D. Antypas hunt for axion-like dark matter with a tabletop magnetometer. Their 2026 arXiv paper reports a broadband search using a radio-frequency rubidium-87 atomic magnetometer. Axion-like particles could form the dark matter that fills the galaxy.

If such a field couples to the spins inside atoms, it would act like a tiny oscillating magnetic field. The magnetometer covers a wide band of frequencies with high sensitivity. A null result still trims the space of allowed couplings. Tabletop searches like this one complement huge detectors at modest cost.
arxiv-2601-09738:
Haley Stone and eleven co-authors link landscape ecology to the risk of wildlife disease outbreaks. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses a heterogeneous graph network for epidemiological reasoning. Estimating how common a pathogen is, and how it spreads, is hard when surveillance data is sparse.

Field data on wildlife disease is detection-driven and unevenly sequenced. The authors build a graph that joins ecological connectivity with case data across space and time. Graph reasoning can fill gaps that raw counts cannot. Better prevalence estimates help agencies target testing and protect both wildlife and people.
arxiv-2601-09838:
Leonie Dyck and a large team describe a robot built to help children recover through play. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents Mobirobot, a socially assistive robot for pediatric therapy. It supports mobilization in children healing from trauma, fractures, or depressive disorders, through personalized exercise programs.

Socially assistive robots can raise engagement in therapy. Success needs more than sound engineering: the design must fit clinics and therapy rooms. Clinicians, therapists, and engineers built it together in short agile cycles. Co-design across settings aims at a robot that busy ward staff will actually use each day.
arxiv-2601-10238:
Stijn Cambie, Andrea Freschi, Patryk Morawski, Kalina Petrova, and Alexey Pokrovskiy bound a Ramsey count. Ramsey counts ask how large a graph must be to force a set shape. Here the shapes are a cycle and a graph of set size. Size is read as the count of edges.

The team prove a clean bound. For each cycle length and each graph with no lone nodes, the count is at most twice the edge count plus half the cycle length. The bound needs the graph to be large next to the cycle. Such bounds pin down how fast forced shapes must show.
arxiv-2601-10338:
Yi Liu and co authors map flaws in add on skills for AI agents. A skill is a pack of rules and code. It can be loaded to give an agent new powers. Such packs run with deep trust. Few checks vet them before use.

That trust gap is a fresh attack field. Bad code in a skill can harm the host. The team ran a large scale test of skills in the wild. They sort the flaws they found by type and risk. The work is a first map of this field. It shows why skill stores need vet steps like app stores.
arxiv-2601-10938:
Xingyu Guo, Cheng Gui, and Zhenbin Wang benchmark universal machine learning potentials for battery kinetics. Faster alkali-ion battery discovery needs accurate models of atomic-scale motion. Shared potentials promise one model for many materials. How far they can be trusted on steep energy landscapes, the terrain of kinetics, is still unsure. The authors test that trust head on.

They compare M3GNet, CHGNet, MACE, SevenNet, GRACE, and Orb against DFT baselines. The test materials are cathodes and solid electrolytes. Kinetics governs charging speed and lifetime, so errors there mislead design the most. The benchmark tells battery modelers which shared tools are ready for kinetic work and which still lag.
arxiv-2601-11238:
David Otero and Javier Parapar work on search quality in this 2026 preprint. Their topic is feedback from first search results, a classic trick. Search fails at times when query words miss the words in texts. Added terms from top hits can close that gap for users.

The classic method, RM3, builds the new query from top-ranked texts. It can drift off topic when early hits are noisy. New work asks large language models to write the added terms. Otero and Parapar test that LLM-assisted path for feedback. The goal is growth of the query with less drift. Good feedback lifts weak first searches at low cost to the user.
arxiv-2601-11438:
Qiaosen Zhang, Matteo Nerini, and Bruno Clerckx solve channel estimation for analog-aided MIMO. Their 2026 letter deals with microwave linear analog computers. Such computers, called MiLACs, aid beamforming in vast MIMO systems. They cut hardware and compute cost by a large share.

Channel estimation for MiLAC systems was an open problem. Classic least squares and MMSE schemes lean on digital math. Heavy digital work would undo the analog gains of MiLACs. The team gives LS and MMSE schemes that fit the hardware. Their schemes keep the estimation light and efficient. That keeps the cost edge of analog beamforming intact. The work clears a key block for gigantic MIMO design.
arxiv-2601-11638:
Josafat Ribeiro Leal Filho and Antonio Augusto Frohlich verify PINN fidelity. Their 2026 preprint uses classical Fisher information for the check. Physics-informed neural networks solve differential equations by learning. They embed physical laws into the training process itself.

Judging how fully a PINN captures dynamics is still hard. Trajectory prediction alone says little about full behavior. The team draws Fisher information from a differentiable system. That quantity can measure sensitivity in the model's fit. A differentiable dynamical system supplies the needed gradients. The method aims at rigorous fidelity scores for PINNs. Such scores matter where PINNs guide real engineering.
arxiv-2601-11838:
Hao Lyu, Jingzheng Wu, Xiang Ling, and their co-authors test a way to find bugs in RISC-V chips. RISC-V is an open design for computer cores. Its open use speeds new chips, but also brings risk of hidden flaws in how cores run code.

Fuzzing feeds odd inputs to a chip to trip flaws. Their tool, named SimFuzz in the work, guides its changes by how alike code blocks are. Smart guidance can reach deep code paths that random tests miss. The work aims to catch flaws before chips ship.
arxiv-2601-12038:
Beishui Liao adds subargument links to a classic frame for argument. Dung's frame judges arguments by attack links alone. It sets aside the inner form of each argument on purpose. That choice made the maths rich, but hides how arguments are built.

Many formal systems need those inner links, most of all when one argument sits inside a larger one. Liao's frame keeps attack links and adds subargument links. That lets the frame track built form while it judges which claims stand. The work links two strands of argument theory.
arxiv-2601-12138:
Abhishek Kumar, Riya Tapwal, and Carsten Maple build a risk taxonomy for language model driving aides. Such aides now sit in cars, where bad or vague advice can cause real harm. It can also breach law or ethics on the road.

Past safety lists are too broad to catch driving risks. Their DriveSafe taxonomy sorts risks by the driving case. A clear list helps teams test aides on road cases before launch. It also helps map which faults are most grave in a car.  A shared list helps car firms test aides the same way.
arxiv-2601-12238:
Sharan Sahu, Cameron J. Hogan, and Martin T. Wells prove that momentum SGD can be shown to be suboptimal for nonstationary problems. They study SGD and its Polyak and Nesterov momentum forms. The task is to track optima that move with time, under strong convexity and smoothness.

Their finite-time bounds split tracking error into three parts. One is transient, one is noise-led, and one is drift-led. That split shows where momentum hurts in a moving task. The result guides choice of optimizer for live systems.  Drift terms grow as the tracked optimum moves more.
arxiv-2601-12438:
Simone Taioli, Francesca Triggiani, and Stefano Simonucci revisit a mismatch in early universe physics. Standard Big Bang theory predicts how much lithium 7 should exist. Old, metal poor stars suggest a far lower value, by a factor of about three to four. This gap is the primordial lithium problem, and it has lasted for years.

Most early lithium 7 was first made as beryllium 7. That beryllium later turned into lithium by electron capture. So the rates of weak and radiative moves for beryllium set the final count. The team recheck those rates with fresh care. If the rates shift, the predicted lithium count shifts too. Their work tests whether nuclear physics alone can close the gap.
arxiv-2601-12538:
Tianxin Wei and a large team survey agentic reasoning in large language models. Reasoning sits under inference, problem solving, and decision making in human thought. Language models reason well in closed worlds, like standard math and code tests. They struggle more in open ended, changing environments where the ground shifts.

The survey tracks the field in three parts named in its title. It covers foundations of agentic reasoning, how the area has evolved, and how agents collaborate. Agentic systems plan, act, and check their own work over many steps. A map of this fast moving field helps builders see what is settled and what is not. It also frames open problems for the next wave of work.
arxiv-2601-12738:
Ba Khiet Le, Zakaria Mazgouri, and Michel Thera study monotonicity for pairs of operators. Monotonicity of a single operator is a classic tool in analysis and optimization. Extending it to pairs helps solve non monotone inclusions, a harder class of problems. Monotone pairs have become an important new tool for such inclusions in recent work.

A key open challenge is how to design the mappings that form a monotone pair. The team also work with a generalized inertial proximal method. Inertial methods add momentum like terms to speed convergence. Pairing the two ideas may yield algorithms for problems once out of reach. The work serves variational analysis and applied optimization.
arxiv-2601-13238:
Chengyin Hu and co-authors craft a rain based attack to test vision language models. Such models train on image and text pairs shot in fair light and clear air. They score well on fair tasks. Their grip in real bad weather is far less known. So is the calm of their image to text match when rain warps a scene.

The attack splits sense parts of a scene, then adds rain in two stages. It aims to show where the match breaks. Weak spots found this way can guide more sound train sets. For teams that ship such models for road or watch use, rain is not a rare edge case. It is a core test.
arxiv-2601-13338:
Ziyi Liu and a large team set out a space where people and many robots talk in plain words first. As homes gain more than one robot, plain speech may be the main way for person to robot and robot to robot talk. Past rigs lean on screens, code, or set commands.

Their space is called a Natural Language Environment. In it, folks and mixed robots plan and act through speech as the shared stream. The paper lays out what such a space needs and how acts flow in it. For home robot teams, a speech first space could cut the learn load for users and let mixed fleets mesh with ease.
arxiv-2601-13538:
Han W. G. and co-authors unscramble weak lens mass maps with a deep net of nested U shapes. Weak lensing bends light from far galaxies by the mass it passes. From that bend, teams map where dark matter lies. True mass maps need a sound inversion of the bend field, a hard step.

Their net is called MIU2Net. It stacks U shaped nets in nests, a form apt for maps at many scales. Next lens surveys will flood teams with bend data. A fast learnt inversion can keep pace where slow rules lag. For dark matter teams, map speed and grade set how much of that flood can be used.
arxiv-2601-14038:
Alexandre Justo Miro and co-authors fix errors in the 3D boxes used to train driverless cars in 2026. Accurate ground truth annotations are critical to supervised learning for vehicles. Cars use active sensors like LiDAR, which scan the surroundings in set patterns. In dynamic scenes, objects are observed at different timestamps and positions.

That timing spread makes 3D box annotation challenging and error-prone. The team works on correcting and quantifying systematic errors in these boxes. Known error sizes let teams judge how much to trust a dataset. Safer self-driving needs labels that match the real world.
arxiv-2601-14538:
Robert L. Bray studies revenue management in this 2026 paper. His model is the simplest one with reusable resources: admission control of two customer classes into a loss queue. A loss queue turns away arrivals when all resources are busy. The model's long-run average collected reward has two natural upper bounds. One is the deterministic relaxation. The other is the full-information offline problem.

Bray's title states his result in formula form. A lookahead of order log N over N is sufficient to bound costs in the overloaded loss network. In plain terms, a short peek ahead nearly matches far costlier schemes. Readers get a sharp limit on how much foresight is worth.
arxiv-2601-14838:
Maram Alwohaibi and four co-authors study a stochastic diffusion equation in this 2026 paper. The equation is a time-space nonlocal diffusion equation driven by additive time-space white noise. Its time derivative is the Caputo derivative of order alpha between zero and two. Fractional derivatives give the process memory: the past keeps weight in the present.

The model couples local diffusion with a nonlocal convolution operator generated by a radial probability density. That coupling incorporates memory effects and long-range spatial interactions. The team studies mild solutions, the weakest solution form that still makes the equation meaningful. The math is hard. It is built for experts who work on noise, chance, and change in one frame. The work stays in the realm of proof. It shows the mild form can be solved, and how. Readers get existence theory for diffusion that remembers and reaches far.
arxiv-2601-14938:
Virginia Falcone, Eleni Prountzou, and co-authors at ETH Zurich build light guides from barium titanate. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with photonic chips, tiny circuits that steer light. Such chips serve in modulators and in sources of paired photons.

Metal oxides suit this work well. They react strongly to electric fields and stay clear across a wide range of colors. Barium titanate stands out for its large Pockels coefficient, a gauge of that response. The team makes its waveguides from a solution-based, liquid route, aimed at compact, efficient on-chip light control.
arxiv-2601-15538:
Himanshu Mishra and Kanwal Mehreen study a clash between two model-editing tools in a 2026 arXiv paper. Machine unlearning removes specific knowledge from a trained model. Targets include copyrighted text and private data. Done well, it avoids the cost of full retraining. Quantization is a separate trick. It shrinks models, often to 4-bit form, so they run cheaply.

The authors find a nasty interaction between the two. Quantization can bring back knowledge that unlearning removed. They describe the effect as catastrophic restoration of forgotten content. Their method, QUAIL, is quantization-aware unlearning, per the title. It aims to keep removals in place after shrinking. For teams that ship small models, the warning is direct. A privacy fix is not done until it survives compression.
arxiv-2601-15838:
Toan Gian and four co-authors compress Wi-Fi sensing data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Wi-Fi sensing estimates human poses without cameras or wearables. It is device-free and privacy-preserving, which makes it attractive. The raw data are channel state information, or CSI. Existing methods process vast amounts of it directly. That volume strains networking resources. Their framework is called TinySense.

TinySense compresses CSI while keeping sensing accurate. The title promises scalability along with accuracy. Human pose estimation is the target task named in the abstract. Homes and clinics could use pose sensing for fall detection and rehab. A compression layer that cuts traffic makes such systems cheaper to run at scale. The work speaks to the wireless sensing community.
arxiv-2601-15938:
Julia Müller and a large team report running a giant xenon detector in a 2026 arXiv paper. Future observatories like XLZD will hunt rare processes in liquid xenon. They need large parts tested in cryogenic xenon first. The PANCAKE facility hosts such tests without shielding. The team operated a shallow dual-phase liquid xenon TPC there. Its inner diameter is 133.4 centimeters, and the chamber is shallow in height.

Stable operation is the headline result. A time projection chamber of this width had to hold steady in liquid xenon. Rare-event searches demand that stability at scale. Every component proven now lowers risk for the full observatories. The paper serves the dark matter and neutrino communities that build these giant detectors.
arxiv-2601-16138:
Zainab Alhathloul and Irfan Ahmad sort Arabic texts by the age they came from. Their 2026 preprint notes how Arabic has changed through time. New words came in, old words fell out, and word use shifted. Those shifts mark old texts from new texts in clear ways. Past work oft splits texts to just old and new age groups.

The pair build a sort tool for texts by time age. Word and style cues guide the sort to the right age. A fine sort helps teams tag large text sets by era. It also aids study of how the tongue changed. The work serves search and care of Arabic text hoards.
arxiv-2601-16438:
Ziwei Zhao, Xiaoni Du and Xingbin Qiao build LCD codes from bent Reed Solomon codes. Their 2026 preprint deals with codes that meet their dual in a null way. LCD means the code and its dual share no word but zero. Such codes guard bits and have clean maths form. The base codes are a bent form of the known GRS codes.

From that base, the team builds two new LCD code sets. Each set rests on a choice of point sets in the base. New sets widen the pool of LCD codes teams can pick. Pool breadth helps match code terms to real links. The work is a build note in code theory.
arxiv-2601-16838:
Emily Hunt and a team of seven co-authors launch a web home for space fans and pros. Space work thrives on talk among peers and with the public. Yet big social sites serve that talk less and less well. Their 2026 preprint sets out Astrosky, a free platform built for this crowd. It stands apart from the big ad-driven sites.

Astrosky joins chat, posts, and outreach in one place. It aims to give space folks a calm, apt home. Pros can share work and news there. Fans can learn and ask in the same halls. The team hopes it keeps the field's talk in its own hands.
arxiv-2601-17238:
Rishi Vanukuru and eight co-authors compare two ways to work with far-off partners. One way is mobile video calls. Calls show real places and objects in real time. The other way is augmented reality, which adds digital content to a live view. The team studies joint work in space across both tools.

They note that calls lose much of the feel of shared space. Moving around and pointing at things is harder on a call. The study looks at how people cope with those limits. It also tests what augmented reality adds or fails to add. The findings can guide tools for remote teams. Good design should keep the sense of place strong.
arxiv-2601-17338:
Hiroshi Onuki, Yukihiro Uchida, and Ryo Yoshizumi build modular polynomials with level structures. The classic modular polynomial links two elliptic curves joined by an isogeny. It has wide use in computational number theory. Point counting on curves is one such use. Computing the polynomial itself is a hard task in its own right.

The authors give a geometric construction for the level case. Level structures add data that many modern algorithms need. A clean construction can make those algorithms faster and safer. Curve-based cryptography rests on such tools. So does research on curve families. The work adds a firm base for both.
arxiv-2601-17638:
Nitin Choudhury and three co-authors present FOCA for malware classification. FOCA fuses audio and visual views of malware data. Most fusion methods work in flat Euclidean space. FOCA works in hyperbolic space instead. That curved space fits hierarchical links between the two views well. Cross-attention joins the streams inside that space.

The authors claim FOCA is first to use that structure for this task. Hierarchy is natural in malware families, which branch like trees. A space that matches that shape can sort samples with more care. Security teams face new malware daily. Better classification speeds response and cuts harm. The work adds a new geometry to the defender's toolkit.
arxiv-2601-18438:
Wei Wang and many colleagues build a tool that grades the sound of made-up speech the way a human ear would. Tests by human ears are slow, dear, and hard to scale, yet new speech tools need grades to grow. Most past tools learned from a thin stock of human grades. That thin stock makes them weak when new kinds of speech show up.

Their tool learns from more than one kind of grade at once. It blends set scores with side by side picks, where a judge says which of two clips sounds best. More kinds of truth make the grades more firm across new data sets. A firm auto grade could let labs test new speech tools fast, with less cost and less wait for human ears.
arxiv-2601-18638:
Tingkai Xue and seven colleagues add doubt counts to the smart design of parts that pick which waves may pass. Such parts, used in chips and in light tools, let some tones through and block the rest. Past smart design was fast but blind to its own doubt. In zones with few past facts, its guesses could be far off, and the search would chase a false peak.

Their plan tracks doubt as it designs, and it steers the search away from zones where doubt is high. Physics rules guide the doubt count, so it stays true to how waves act. A search that knows its doubt should land on parts that work in the lab, not just on screen. That gain counts for parts that are dear to make and test.
arxiv-2601-18738:
Yifan Jing, Cosmin Pohoata, and Max Wenqiang Xu study when a sparse set of whole counts must still hold a neat pattern. The set is banned from a graph shape: no group in it may form a full web of a set size in two parts. Sets that shun such webs can still be quite thick by count. The team ask if a thick set of that kind must hold a full solve of a plain sum task.

The task must stay the same when all its counts are shifted by one step. The team show that a thick banned set holds such a solve for each sum task of five or more counts. That is a strong claim: a ban on one shape can't kill all neat sum forms. It ties the maths of graphs to the maths of sums in a fresh way.
arxiv-2601-18938:
Xin Qiao and seven co-authors fill in missing node features in graphs when most data is gone. Graphs store facts as node features, but real graphs often lose many of them. Older methods, built on hidden features or broad spread, give shaky guesses and can pass errors along the graph.

Their method, FSD-CAP, works in two stages to lift the quality of the filled in values. It spreads facts across parts of the graph while staying aware of each node's class. Better fills under extreme sparsity matter wherever graphs are built from patchy records, from social data to molecule sets.
arxiv-2601-19038:
Long Chen and four co-authors speed up mirror descent, a method that bends downhill search around a space's shape. A mirror function encodes the shape and the limits of the space, which keeps steps valid while they converge. Speeded up forms of the method exist, drawn from a system of differential equations.

The team derives their version by splitting the work into a variable part and an operator part. Splitting lets each piece be handled by the tool that fits it best. The result is a faster method with the same kind of guarantees, aimed at large problems where shape and limits matter.
arxiv-2601-19738:
Daniele Lizzio Bosco and three colleagues work on making quantum circuits cheaper to run. Fault-tolerant quantum computers build circuits from Clifford gates plus T gates. The T gates dominate the cost, so cutting their number can decide whether a circuit runs at all. Compiling a circuit into this gate set with few T gates is a central task.

The authors propose pre-synthesis: learning small local edits to a circuit before the main compilation. Local edits that lower the T-count are found by learning, then applied across the circuit. Even modest savings multiply over large computations. The approach sits before standard synthesis in the toolchain. It offers a new lever for the resource problem in fault-tolerant computing.
arxiv-2601-20138:
Richard Csaky scales up next-token prediction for MEG, a method that records magnetic fields from brain activity. His model works in source space, on signals mapped to locations in the brain. It is trained on a corpus of over five hundred hours and thousands of sessions, drawn from the three largest MEG datasets.

A modified vector quantizer turns the many channels of MEG into a flat stream of tokens. A Qwen2-based model then learns to predict the next token across long contexts and across scanners. Large models of brain signals could support tools that read neural activity and compare recordings between labs.
arxiv-2601-20238:
Gavin Wang and four colleagues study how the release of ChatGPT changed political talk on Reddit's largest political forum. They examine ideological and emotional patterns across millions of comments. Their analysis shows that ideological polarization grew after the release: liberal-leaning authors posted still more liberal comments, and conservative-leaning authors posted still more conservative ones.

The title states the paired finding: models polarize users ideologically but moderate them affectively, in tone. That split matters for how platforms judge AI's effect on public debate. A tool can calm the mood of a thread while quietly pushing its sides further apart.
arxiv-2601-20338:
Nam V. Tran builds a neural network method for solving generalized monotone inclusion problems, a broad class in optimization and equilibrium theory. The method rests on a forward-backward splitting dynamical framework. It is designed so that solutions are reached within a predefined time, a property called predefined-time stability.

The problems are set in Hilbert spaces, with one maximal set-valued operator and one single-valued mapping. Guarantees of arrival by a chosen time are rare and valuable in control, where deadlines are real. The paper adds applications that show where such timed solvers can be used.
arxiv-2601-20438:
Ailsa Keating, Ivan Smith, and Michael Wemyss survey examples where symplectic monodromy splits off the symplectic mapping class group. Symplectic geometry studies spaces with a structure that tracks area, and monodromy describes how that structure twists around a family of spaces. In some cases the twist separates cleanly from the rest of the mapping class group.

The authors use the examples to display different techniques and inputs for such arguments. Along the way they state several open questions and conjectures. A survey of this kind gives researchers a map of a subtle corner of geometry, and of where its proofs still run out.
arxiv-2601-20538:
Ling Tang and six colleagues study how to interpret extreme events that emerge in systems of interacting language model agents. Such multi-agent systems can simulate complex human-like behavior. Their interactions sometimes produce extreme events whose origins stay hidden inside the black box of emergence.

Interpreting those events is critical for system safety, the authors argue. If a simulation of markets or crowds suddenly tips into a crash or a panic, operators need to know which interactions drove it. Their work aims at tracing emergence back to causes that can be checked and governed.
arxiv-2601-20738:
Dawit Kiros Redie, Reza Arablouei, and Stefan Werner work on making federated learning cheaper to run. Their 2026 paper concerns training shared across many devices. Each device trains locally and sends updates, not raw data. To cut traffic, updates are compressed. Error feedback stores what compression dropped and adds it back later.

The catch appears when data differ across devices, the non-IID case. The stored error can decay too slowly. That leaves a gradient mismatch and stalls progress in the early rounds. The authors propose SA-PEF, which joins step-ahead correction with partial error feedback. The method aims to keep early training moving despite compression. It speaks to teams training models across split data sources that do not match.
arxiv-2601-20838:
Brian Christian and six co-authors show that the judges of AI carry biases from their own upbringing. Their 2026 paper studies reward models, the scorers at the heart of AI alignment. Reward models are central to aligning large language models with human values. Yet they have received less attention than the models they guide. A reward model starts life as a pretrained language model. It therefore inherits representations that shape its behavior.

The authors ask how deep that inheritance runs. Values absorbed during pretraining may tilt what the reward model favors. That tilt then steers every model trained under its scores. The paper examines the nature and extent of this influence. Its findings matter for anyone who treats reward models as neutral judges. They begin biased, and the study measures the bias.
arxiv-2601-21038:
Barbara Kaltenbacher proves that solutions of a slow diffusion equation settle to a steady state. Her 2026 paper studies a nonlinear subdiffusion equation with two counteracting terms. Subdiffusion spreads more slowly than normal diffusion. The equation pairs that slow spread with a spatial operator and two rival effects. One term pushes growth; the other pulls it back. A source term completes the balance.

The result gives decay rates to equilibrium as time grows. Rates matter: they tell how fast a system forgets its start. The proof handles the fractional time derivative that makes subdiffusion hard. Such equations model transport in crowded, sticky media. Knowing the pull toward equilibrium helps predict long-run behavior. The paper is a rigorous analysis aimed at specialists in partial differential equations.
arxiv-2601-21138:
Noah Dasanaike builds a record linkage method that needs no labeled training data. The 2026 paper presents EnsembleLink. Record linkage matches records that refer to the same entity across datasets. It is essential to empirical social science. Yet it remains methodologically underdeveloped. Researchers often treat it as a preprocessing step. They apply ad hoc rules and never quantify the uncertainty that linkage errors add downstream.

Existing methods force a bad choice. They either achieve low accuracy or demand substantial labeled training data. An ensemble approach can sidestep that trade-off. Combining several weak linkers can yield a strong one. EnsembleLink aims for accuracy without the labeling burden. Cleaner linkage means cleaner conclusions in studies that merge records. The paper upgrades a quiet but vital step of data work.
arxiv-2601-21238:
Xuewen Liu, Zhikai Li, Jing Zhang, Mengjuan Chen, and Qingyi Gu study how to shrink a class of image-making models without ruining them. These models build pictures step by step, much like language models build text. Shrinking a model by using fewer bits per number cuts its size and speeds it up.

That trick is well tested on other networks but barely tried here. The authors show that standard shrinking methods do not carry over well to this model type. Their method adapts the process to how these models actually generate images. The goal is smaller, faster models that still produce output of the same quality.
arxiv-2601-21338:
Ji-Xuan He and five co-authors improve the sharpening of hyperspectral images. These images record many narrow color bands, which reveal material details normal photos miss. Raising the spatial detail while keeping the colors true is the core challenge.

Recent methods lean on spatial patterns and often neglect how bands relate to each other. That neglect can cause false wiggles in the spectra and results that break physics. Their plug-in module refines the spectra inside existing models. Any current method can adopt it without a rebuild. Truer spectra matter for farming, geology, and environmental checks from aircraft and satellites.
arxiv-2601-21538:
Ruifeng Zheng and Yanqing Xu study how primordial black holes could form from the early universe's inflation. Such holes need very large density bumps to collapse under their own gravity. Those same bumps would also stir gravitational waves that detectors might hear.

The authors join two known inflation models with a local coupling of a special shape. The coupling briefly breaks the slow roll that keeps inflation smooth. That break is what lets the bumps grow large enough. The study links black hole births to a wave signal, giving observers a paired prediction to test.
arxiv-2601-21638:
Mingji Deng, Cuihua Du, Jian Zhang, HaoYang Liu, and ZhongCheng Li build a lighter model of the Milky Way that explains its warped disk. Warps, where the disk bends like a hat brim, can grow out of galaxy mergers. Recent work also shows the galaxy's rotation curve dropping off in a way heavier models do not predict.

The authors construct a merger model based on the known Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus event. That ancient merger is a prime suspect for stirring our galaxy. A low-mass model that matches both the warp and the rotation curve would revise estimates of the galaxy's dark matter. It also sharpens the story of how the Milky Way was assembled.
arxiv-2601-21838:
Weizhou Cai and co-authors report progress on protecting quantum information with bosonic codes. Quantum error correction is the foundation of any future fault-tolerant quantum computer. Yet corrected logical qubits so far live only about twice as long as their best physical parts, a disappointingly small gain.

The team argues that the main barrier is not the coherence of the cavities that hold the information. Instead, errors introduced by the ancilla, a helper system used during operations, do the damage. Their 2026 preprint presents error-detectable universal control aimed at high-gain bosonic correction. If operational errors can be caught and curbed, bosonic codes could finally deliver the large gains their theory has long promised.
arxiv-2601-22038:
Vitalii Aksenov, Martin Eigel, and Mathias Oster speed up sums that deal with chance curves. Many tasks in stats can be cast as fixed-point sums. You run the same step again and again till the result stops moving. One key use is to find the mean of a set of chance curves, in a sense set by the Wasserstein gap.

Plain runs of such steps can be slow. The team tries a speed-up trick called Anderson mixing. They test it in the space of bell-shaped curves, where gaps and means have neat closed forms. Fast solvers of this kind help in Bayes work and in training AI models. In both, these sums run deep in the loop, and their cost is paid on each run.
arxiv-2601-22238:
Erik Aver and a large team present a fresh value for how much helium the Big Bang left behind. Their 2026 preprint is part four of a project built on the Large Binocular Telescope. The team took clean new data from a set of gas clouds poor in heavy elements.

All clouds were watched and worked through in the same way. The team also updated key steps, such as the glow rates used for helium. A firm early value tests the standard story of the cosmos. It also guides work on how the first elements formed. The clouds act as near time capsules.
arxiv-2601-22438:
Shangshu Qian and four co-authors make model serving bounce back fast when hardware fails. Their 2026 preprint, KevlarFlow, notes that big clusters fail often, and one fault can down a whole service. Old recovery can take ten minutes, as gear restarts and huge weights reload.

KevlarFlow aims to cut that dead time to a small part of the old span. Fast recovery keeps chat and search tools live for users. It also saves the vast cost of idle chips. The work is a shield for the serving layer. It treats faults as routine, not rare.
arxiv-2601-22538:
Yannis Montreuil and four co-authors study when a forecaster should hand a call to a human expert as conditions drift. Their 2026 preprint works on non-stationary time series, where the pattern shifts over time. Feedback is partial: the router sees only the picked expert's call, and the pool of experts changes.

They model signed expert errors with a switching state-space model. That model tracks who is hot as regimes change. Smart hand-offs can lift accuracy while saving expert time. The work fits streams like energy, health, and finance. That saving can be large at scale.
arxiv-2601-22638:
Palash Goyal and a team built ScholarPeer, a multi-agent system that reviews papers with context, not in a vacuum. Auto review has grown from sorting text to writing structured feedback. Their 2026 preprint notes that top systems still give surface notes, and miss novelty and deep method flaws.

ScholarPeer checks a paper against its field, so praise and blame rest on what is truly new. Deeper reviews could ease the load on human referees. They must still be watched for error and bias. The work aims at review that reads like a peer.
arxiv-2601-22738:
Han Wang and four co-authors built StreamSense, a live monitor that reads social cues in streams and calls in a big model only when needed. Live platforms must react to social signals in real time, from partial video, text, and audio that arrive out of sync. Their 2026 preprint pairs a light streaming encoder with selective routing.

Hard cases go to a vision-language expert; easy ones stay cheap. That split keeps the watch both fast and sharp. The work serves safety and community teams on live platforms. It spends big-model effort where it counts.
arxiv-2601-23138:
Duván Cardona, William Obeng-Denteh, and Frederick Opoku study hyperbolic equations with complex characteristics on Fourier Lebesgue spaces. These spaces measure functions through their frequency content, with flexible integrability. Well-posedness asks whether solutions exist, are unique, and depend steadily on the data.

Their harmonic analysis approach first bounds Fourier integral operators with complex phase on several function spaces. Those bounds then carry over to the differential equations. Such results support models of wave motion in settings beyond the classical theory. Besov and Triebel-Lizorkin spaces are included alongside Fourier Lebesgue spaces, widening the result's reach in harmonic analysis.
