Those two show how fuel shifts drive the fatal turn. Boosting the system may treat some diseases, the authors note. Shifts between death modes may serve cancer care in new ways.
europmc-pmc10561438:
Chehelgerdi and a large team reviewed nanotechnology for targeted cancer care in 2023. Tiny carriers can ferry drugs straight to tumour cells. Fresh work in protein design and materials has spawned new ways to aim them. Hope runs high among patients and labs alike.

Yet the path to clinics is steep, Chehelgerdi reports. Many carriers won approval for human trials, but only a few gained full clearance for use. The review lists the cleared products and the hurdles each one cleared. Hurdles span body safety, factory scale-up, and weak gains in real patients. The authors back more work to close the lab-to-clinic gap.
europmc-pmc10628838:
Belloy and co-authors ran a gene study in 2023 on APOE and Alzheimer disease risk. APOE is a gene that comes in forms which raise or lower the risk of this memory disease. The best-known risk form is called epsilon 4. Past work hints that its effect is not the same in each group of people.

The study tests the gene's links to risk across age bands and sex. It also splits people by race and ethnicity, and by global population ancestry. Those splits matter, since the gene's forms vary in frequency and force across ancestries. Belloy aims to show where the risk holds firm and where it shifts. Such maps can guide fair risk checks for each group.
europmc-pmc10689838:
Koh and co-authors reviewed CD8 T cell subsets in 2023, a branch of killer immune cells. These cells hunt infected or cancerous cells and kill them. After they meet a target, plain CD8 cells gain skills to strike. The classic view held one main killer subset.

Fresh proof splits the killers into distinct subsets, Koh reports. Each subset has its own mix of attack signals and toxic parcels. Each also plays a distinct part in infection, cancer, and other diseases. That split may explain why some immune drugs help one patient and miss the next. Drugs tuned to one subset could sharpen care, the authors argue. The review maps each subset and its known jobs.
europmc-pmc11023938:
Lu and colleagues show that pain-sensing nerves help wounds heal by steering immune cells in this 2024 study. Tissue healing depends heavily on the immune system, and healing falters in diabetes and old age. Nociceptors are sensory nerve cells that detect harm. Their role in repair after sudden injury was unclear.

Removing a key pain nerve channel in mice impaired skin wound repair and muscle regrowth, the team found. Nerve endings grew into the injured tissue and released a signal called CGRP. That signal acted on neutrophils and macrophages, two immune cell types, to cut recruitment and speed cell clean-up. It pushed macrophages toward a repair form. Giving an engineered form of the signal sped healing in mice lacking the nerves and in diabetic mice.
europmc-pmc11115438:
Cossarizza and a very large panel present the third edition of flow cytometry guidelines in this 2021 document. Flow cytometry runs cells past lasers to read their traits one by one, and cell sorting then separates chosen cells. It is a core method in immunology, the study of the immune system. The guidelines state what to consider when planning such experiments.

Sections describe the traits and functional tests for all major human and mouse immune cell subsets. Tables flag where human and mouse cells differ, a common source of error. Clinical samples get full treatment, with examples from autoimmune diseases, cancers, and acute and chronic infections. A section on tips, tricks, and pitfalls collects practical warnings. All parts were written and peer-reviewed by leading experts, the authors note.
europmc-pmc11223838:
Letunic and Bork present version 6 of a web tool for drawing and annotating family trees of species in this 2024 paper. Phylogenetic trees show how species relate through evolution. The Interactive Tree Of Life, or iTOL, is a free online tool to manage, display, and annotate such trees. It is open to everyone.

Version 6 brings a modernised, fully rewritten interface, the authors report. A new dataset type shows coloured and labelled ranges along branches. Templates can now assign notes to many nodes at once using text matching, including full pattern expressions. Node metadata gained new display and export options and can be edited in bulk. Labels support several font styles at once with precise placement. Automatic taxonomy assignment, which names nodes from a reference, was extended.
europmc-pmc11701638:
Dyer and a very large team present Ensembl 2025, the annual update of a genome data platform, in this paper. Ensembl integrates public genomics data from across the tree of life, focusing on species tied to human health, agriculture, and biodiversity. Expansion continued this year, with more than 4,800 eukaryotic and over 31,300 prokaryotic genomes on offer.

The new Ensembl site, still in beta, now holds over 2,700 eukaryotic genome assemblies. It provides views of genomes, genes, transcripts, variation, and homology, meaning comparisons of genes across species. It will replace the current rapid release site as a step toward a single integrated site. Regulatory annotation improved for human, mouse, and agricultural species. The Variant Effect Predictor tool, which forecasts what a DNA change does, was expanded. Training and documentation programmes accompany the release.
europmc-pmc12535838:
GBD 2023 Causes of Death Collaborators catalogued causes of death worldwide in 2025. Timely death data by age, sex, and place shape health policy. The analysis spans 204 countries and territories. It also covers 660 subnational locations from 1990 to 2023.

Estimates cover 292 causes of death for each year. A modeling ensemble produced most cause-specific death rates. Years of life lost were computed from death counts per cause. New measures add the chance of dying before age 70. GBD 2023 Causes of Death Collaborators also report mean age at death by cause. Most death rates came from a model ensemble the team calls CODEm.
europmc-pmc1273638:
Monticelli and colleagues profiled microRNAs across mouse blood cells in 2005. MicroRNAs are small RNAs that dial down gene output. Their patterns in the blood-forming system were unmapped. The study gives the first systematic profile for those cells.

Profiles differed sharply between blood cell types. Beyond guiding which lineage a cell joins, patterns marked cell identity. The authors suggest microRNAs help lock in differentiation states. Monticelli supplies a baseline atlas for blood development studies. Later work can compare disease states against this map. It appeared in Genome Biology in 2005. Mature microRNAs run just 19 to 22 letters long and recur across many species.
europmc-pmc1440938:
Garlic mustard, a plant from Europe, now spreads through North American woods. Stinson and co-authors asked in 2006 how it beats local trees. They found the invader leaks fungus-fighting compounds into the soil. Those compounds break the bond between young trees and root fungi that help them feed.

Such fungi, called arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, trade soil nutrients for plant sugars. With the bond cut, native seedlings grew poorly. Stinson argues this hidden attack may explain why garlic mustard thrives in calm, undisturbed woods. The study shows an invader can harm locals without touching them, by cutting the links they rely on.
europmc-pmc1464138:
Naming a small molecule from its mass alone is harder than it sounds. Kind and Fiehn made that point in 2006 for metabolomics, the study of all small molecules in a sample. Even with mass errors under one part per million, many formulas fit a single reading at higher masses.

The pair showed with math that a second clue fixes the problem. The pattern of isotopes, heavier forms of the same atoms, rules out over 95 percent of false formulas. Kind compared eight chemical databases for the task. Their scripts, shared free online, can shrink thousands of candidate formulas to a short list.
europmc-pmc1764438:
Algorithms can learn gene regulation from expression data, but genome-scale proof was missing. Faith and co-authors supplied it in 2007 for E. coli, using 445 expression arrays and 3,216 known regulatory links. They tested four algorithm classes and added their own, CLR.

CLR beat the next best method by 36 percent in average precision. At a setting catching 60 percent of true links, it proposed 1,079 interactions, 741 of them novel. Lab tests confirmed 21 new links for three regulators. One found link ties iron transport to central metabolism, confirmed by gene measurements. Faith offers the data set as a benchmark for the field.
europmc-pmc1887538:
Swindell, Huebner and Weber profiled in 2007 how a plant's heat shock system answers many stresses besides heat. In Arabidopsis, the heat response runs through four families of heat shock proteins and a set of 21 known transcription factors. Those same proteins also react to other hardships, but the overlap map was missing.

The team measured gene activity for all those factors and proteins across ten treatments: heat, cold, salt, drought, osmotic stress, DNA damage, ultraviolet light, oxidative stress, wounding, and infection. Samples covered both shoots and roots. Every treatment touched the heat pathways to some degree, showing wide cross-talk. Heat, cold, salt, and osmotic stress switched the system on most strongly. Other stresses gave narrower replies that varied by protein family and tissue. The heat network doubles as a general stress hub.
europmc-pmc1929138:
Herschkowitz, Perou and co-authors compared in 2007 the gene activity patterns of mouse mammary tumors with human breast cancers. Human breast tumors fall into at least three major subtypes with different outcomes, plus a normal-like group. Mouse models are used to study and test treatments for these subtypes, but only if they truly match.

The team profiled tumors from thirteen mouse models on microarrays and set them beside human tumor data. Many defining traits of the human subtypes were conserved in the mouse models. The hormone receptor negative subtypes, one marked by high HER2 levels and one resembling basal cells, had mouse counterparts. So did the receptor positive luminal subtype, which splits into better and worse outcome groups. The match validates specific mouse models for specific human diseases, rather than breast cancer in general.
europmc-pmc2022638:
Roberts and co-workers studied in 2007 whether living near farm pesticide spraying during pregnancy links to autism. They identified 465 children with autism spectrum disorders born in 1996 to 1998 in California's Central Valley. Controls were 6,975 healthy term infants matched on timing. Official spray records and land maps showed how close mothers lived to applications during pregnancy.

Out of 249 hypotheses tested, four survived strict checks against false positives. All involved organochlorine pesticides, mainly dicofol and endosulfan, sprayed during weeks one to eight of pregnancy. That is when the central nervous system first forms. Mothers within 500 metres of the heaviest spraying had an odds ratio of 6.1, and risk rose with amount sprayed. The authors call for further study.
europmc-pmc2125538: A medical paper on Spirochaeta morsus muris, the cause of rat-bite fever, second paper. The rat-bite germ. This article preserves that bacteriology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2128338: Part of a streptococcus culture went soft in this study, losing its power to burst red blood cells. The researchers tracked the fading hemolysis. The weakened strain's story, recorded. The article preserves that bacteriology research.
europmc-pmc2128538: A medical paper on fat metabolism in nephritis. The kidney's fat. This article preserves that nephrology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2130938: A medical paper on microbic virulence and host susceptibility in paratyphoid infection. The germ's strength again. This article preserves that bacteriology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2131138: A medical paper on normal and pathological fragmentation of red blood cells. The broken cells. This article preserves that hematology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2131438: A medical paper on effect of formalin on the virus of vesicular stomatitis of horses. The pickled virus. This article preserves that virology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2131638: A medical paper with studies of tissue maintenance, persisting bloodlessness after functional changes. The bloodless tissue again. This article preserves that physiology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2134938:
Miska and a large team deleted most microRNA genes in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans in 2007 to test their importance. MicroRNAs are short non-coding RNAs that repress gene expression after copying. The team created deletions in 87 microRNA genes. Together with earlier mutants, that covered 95 genes, or 83 percent of known worm microRNAs. Each mutant was checked for survival and visible development defects.

The majority of microRNAs proved individually non-essential for viability or development. Most deletions caused no grossly abnormal traits at all. That pattern fits the idea of redundancy, where microRNAs or their pathways back each other up. Losing one is then buffered by others. The study is the first comprehensive genetic analysis of microRNA function in any organism. The mutant set forms a permanent resource for systematic study.
europmc-pmc2140338: A biology paper on the effect of various acids on the digestion of proteins by pepsin. The acidic digestion. This article preserves that biochemistry. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2140638: A biology paper on hydrogen ion concentrations within the alimentary tract of insects. The bugs' gut acid. This article preserves that entomology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2180238: A medical paper on the effect of pulmonary congestion on the ventilation of the lungs. The congested breath. This article preserves that pulmonology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2254638:
Hoogewijs and co-workers validated reference genes in 2008 for gene expression studies of antioxidant sod genes in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans. Accurate measurement needs normalisation against genes whose expression stays constant. No validated set existed for this worm, a key model for insulin signalling, lifespan and stress research. The team tested twelve candidate reference genes by quantitative PCR across wild-type worms, three insulin-pathway mutants, dormant dauer larvae and third-stage larvae.

Three genes, pmp-3, Y45F10D.4 and cdc-42, showed the most stable expression and were used for normalisation. With them, sod-1 and sod-3 levels differed significantly in daf-2 mutants versus normal worms. In dauer larvae, four sod genes differed from third-stage larvae. The authors stress that stable reference genes are essential for reliable quantification, and that their method transfers to other worm studies.
europmc-pmc2323238:
Tomancak and colleagues mapped gene activity across fruit fly embryos in this 2007 atlas study. Drosophila melanogaster is the fruit fly used in much genetics research. Knowing where and when each gene is switched on helps explain how an embryo builds tissues.

The team documented activity patterns for 6,003 genes, which is 44% of the 13,659 protein-coding genes in the fly genome. They used a staining method that shows gene activity in place, inside the whole embryo. About 40% of the genes they recorded were active only in certain tissues, not throughout the body. The rest were active more broadly. The atlas gave researchers a shared reference for comparing embryo development across genes.
europmc-pmc2446438:
Horvath and Dong gave gene network analysis a geometric reading in 2008. Coexpression networks link genes whose activity rises and falls together across samples. Biologists borrowed the network language but used only a thin slice of it, while statisticians analysing the same data spoke a different dialect.

The authors built a rough dictionary between the two fields. The bridge is geometry: correlations between genes behave like angles between arrows, so network ideas such as connectivity get precise visual meanings. They showed when a network's link matrix splits neatly into per-gene contributions, a property they call approximate factorizability. Hub genes, the most connected ones, can then be read against sample traits, and a gene's connectivity inside its module doubles as a fuzzy membership score. Examples came from human, mouse, and yeast data sets.
europmc-pmc2447538:
Mostafavi and colleagues built a gene function predictor fast enough to run live in 2008. Most genes still have no known job, and computer methods guess jobs by merging many data sets linking genes that work together. The most accurate methods took so long that their predictions sat in ageing static databases.

Their algorithm, GeneMANIA, blends several association networks with a fast method derived from ridge regression, a standard statistical fit. It then spreads known labels across a process-specific network. On a mouse benchmark and a new yeast benchmark it matched or beat the leading methods. It also shrugged off redundant or irrelevant input data. Each prediction took under ten seconds on average in their tests. A prototype web server let users query it in real time rather than downloading frozen results.
europmc-pmc2529338:
Tao, Fang, Alroy, and Sahagian improved a mouse model of late-stage breast cancer in this 2008 paper. The 4T1 tumour line is valued because it spreads to the same organs as human breast cancer, but tracking it inside living animals was hard. The team engineered two versions of the line to glow with firefly luciferase, a light-producing enzyme, so cameras could follow them.

Tumours grew in two phases, and spread appeared in the second phase, five to six weeks after implantation. A mid-course shrinkage coincided with tissue death and a rush of immune cells, and it vanished in mice lacking adaptive immunity, showing the immune system caused it. Gene analysis linked the spreading behaviour to secreted factors that build blood vessels, reshape tissue, and recruit immune cells. Blood-forming activity in spleen and liver also rose steadily.
europmc-pmc2575538:
Wirapati and colleagues performed in 2008 the largest meta-analysis then done of gene activity signatures in breast cancer, pooling 2,833 tumours. Many published signatures claimed to predict patient outcome, yet they shared almost no genes, which puzzled the field. The team organised genes by three biological processes: cell proliferation, estrogen receptor signalling, and HER2 signalling.

All nine prognostic signatures they tested performed about equally well. Their power came mostly from detecting proliferation, how fast tumour cells divide. The known tumour subtypes mapped cleanly onto the three process modules, from basal-like to HER2-like to the two luminal types. Being estrogen-receptor negative or HER2 positive predicted poor outcome mainly because those tumours proliferate more. Tumour size and lymph node status still added information of their own, beyond the genes.
europmc-pmc2684638:
Sella and co-authors reviewed in 2009 growing proof that natural selection shapes far more of the fruit fly genome than textbooks assumed. The classic view held that most DNA change is neutral drift, with adaptation rare and the functional share of the genome small. New data from comparing variation within fly species and differences between them told a busier story.

Much of the fly genome, they report, sits under purifying selection, selection that weeds out damage, which means it does something that matters. A large share of the differences between species, in coding and noncoding DNA alike, look adaptive rather than accidental. Selection may be so common that neutral changes ride or fall with adaptive neighbors they happen to sit beside. The shift reaches beyond flies: conservation work and genome analysis alike must reckon with a genome largely under selection's hand.
europmc-pmc2774338:
Gregory and co-authors reported in 2009 genomic and epigenetic evidence tying the oxytocin receptor gene, OXTR, to autism. Autism is strongly heritable, yet single-gene causes explain under a tenth of cases. They scanned one hundred nineteen people from families with several autistic members. They hunted for deleted or duplicated DNA stretches. Then they studied how the gene is switched off by methylation, a chemical tag on DNA.

One autistic child carried a deletion removing OXTR, shared with his mother, who had obsessive-compulsive symptoms. His affected sibling lacked the deletion. Instead, that sibling showed abnormal silencing of the gene by methylation. Across separate blood and brain samples, autistic people showed higher methylation at several sites in the gene's control island. Brain tissue from autistic donors also made less OXTR message. Both loss and silencing of this receptor, they argue, can feed into autism.
europmc-pmc2788538:
Shankar and Walsh reviewed in 2009 synaptic dysfunction and the amyloid beta protein in Alzheimer's disease. Loss of synapses, the junctions between brain cells, is an early and constant feature of the disease. Its extent tracks the severity of dementia closely. That link suggests synapse failure drives the early memory loss, and that lasting disruption of plasticity may later kill cells outright.

Wide-ranging research implicates amyloid beta in causing the disease. The harmful forms, on the evidence, are not the stiff fibers of plaques but small soluble clusters that float between cells. These non-fibrillar forms appear to compromise synapses directly. The review gathers the evidence for that case and walks through possible mechanisms of this synaptotoxicity, how the clusters might jam signaling and weaken connections. It ends with points where drugs might intervene against the process.
europmc-pmc2792038:
Lin and colleagues asked how a vaccine can protect mice against two very unlike bloodstream invaders at once: the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus and the fungus Candida albicans. Their 2009 vaccine used a piece of a Candida surface protein, called rAls3p-N, mixed with a standard booster chemical.

Protection needed two signals from helper T cells, named IFN-gamma and IL-17A, plus working eater cells that destroy germs. Vaccinated mice made three T-cell types that released these signals, drew more eater cells into infected tissue, and cleared both germs faster. Blocking the IL-17A signal likewise left ordinary mice open to both infections. Mice lacking IFN-gamma stayed prone to both infections, showing one shared defense covers both.
europmc-pmc2820538:
Coppé and colleagues found in 2010 that mouse cells only mimic the human aging-cell secretions when grown at body-like oxygen levels. Senescent cells, which have stopped dividing for good, release a cocktail of signals called the SASP that changes how neighbors behave. Mouse cells grown at standard lab oxygen, twenty percent, arrested but secreted almost none of it.

Grown at three percent oxygen, which matches body tissue, and pushed into senescence by radiation, mouse cells produced a robust human-like cocktail. Both species raised tissue-cutting enzymes from one shared gene cluster. A single factor, CXCL-1, did most of the work of making nearby precancer cells grow, and only low-oxygen mouse cells fed tumor growth in animals.
europmc-pmc2867938:
De Santa and colleagues reported in 2010 that much of the genome's activity outside genes happens exactly at its control switches. Mammalian DNA is copied into RNA in many places beyond known genes, and some of that RNA comes from enhancers, stretches that boost gene activity. The team mapped where the copying enzyme RNA polymerase II sits across the genome in immune cells.

A large share of the outside-gene copying sites landed precisely on enhancers, and the enhancers themselves were being transcribed. That copying rose when the cells were stimulated, tying it to active gene control rather than stray noise. The finding suggests the short RNAs made at enhancers deserve study as part of how genes are switched on, and it helps annotate what the vast non-gene genome is doing.
europmc-pmc2998438:
Yang and Hekimi reported in 2010 that a burst of a reactive oxygen signal from mitochondria can lengthen life in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans. Mitochondrial oxidants are usually cast as ageing toxins, yet several long-lived worm mutants carry faulty mitochondria.

Reviewing that mutant evidence, they argue the oxidant superoxide works as a stress signal that switches on defences, rather than only as damage. Mutations that mildly impair the power chain raise the signal and extend lifespan, while stronger faults shorten it. The reframing helps explain why some antioxidant treatments fail to slow ageing and why mild stress can protect.
europmc-pmc3017038:
Ferrer-Vaquer and colleagues engineered a mouse strain that lights up wherever a key development signal, Wnt, is active, in a 2010 study. Watching embryos develop live needs reporters bright and sharp enough to resolve single cells, and existing Wnt reporters fell short.

They placed six signal-responsive switches ahead of a glowing protein fused to a nuclear anchor, so active cells shine as bright dots. In embryos and adults the glow appeared exactly at known Wnt sites, discretely and specifically. The strain gives developmental biologists a crisp live readout for filming how signals guide shaping of the body.
europmc-pmc3035538:
Sulaiman and coauthors asked in 2003 whether a gut parasite found in animals can also infect people. The parasite, Giardia duodenalis, causes diarrhea worldwide and looks the same under the microscope whether it comes from a person, a dog, or a cow. The team read one gene from parasites taken from people and from several animal hosts to sort them into family groups.

Most host types carried their own distinct parasite lines. One large group, however, mixed most human samples with those from muskrats and beavers, plus a rabbit sample. That mixing shows parasites from some animals can plausibly reach people through water or contact. The gene test also gives health workers a way to tell parasite types apart. Such typing can trace outbreak sources and sharpen the classification of this messy parasite group.
europmc-pmc3069738:
Winn and many coauthors gave in 2011 an overview of CCP4, the shared software suite that structural biologists use to solve molecular structures from X ray crystal data. The project, run as a community collaboration since the nineteen nineties, gathers around two hundred programs from many labs into one package with common file formats. It serves academic and commercial researchers alike.

The overview traces how the suite grew, what it can do today, and what is planned for its next generation. Shared libraries and a graphical interface let separate programs hand results to each other smoothly. A user can go from raw diffraction images to a finished structure in one environment. Training and education are part of the mission. The paper serves as the standard reference for citing the suite as a whole.
europmc-pmc3084838:
Masliah and coauthors showed in 2011 that antibody treatment can ease brain disease in a mouse model of Lewy body disorders, which include Parkinson disease and a common dementia. Both involve clumps of a protein called alpha-synuclein in neurons. The team gave model mice a lab made antibody aimed at the protein's tail end, by passive immunization rather than vaccination.

Treated mice performed better in a water maze that tests memory and navigation. Their brains held less of a harmful cut form of the protein in axons and synapses, and the related nerve damage was reduced. Tracking studies showed the antibody entered the brain, latched onto cells carrying the clumps, and routed the protein to the cell's disposal system. The authors argue the approach deserves development for patients. Antibodies against this protein have since become a major drug strategy.
europmc-pmc3185738:
Patrick Woo and colleagues surveyed coronavirus genomes with computer analysis in a 2010 paper in Viruses. A surge of newly found coronaviruses in animals and people, including the SARS virus, finally allowed family-wide comparison. These viruses carry the largest genomes of any RNA virus, and their base composition varies widely between members.

The family sorts into three established genera, with a fourth emerging from bird viruses. Dating analysis placed the shared ancestor of SARS-related viruses only a few years before the outbreak, evolving at a brisk clip. Genome shuffling between strains proved common, even across species, and letter-usage bias bore the marks of two distinct pressures. The review maps the family's structure and habits for future outbreak science.
europmc-pmc3219338:
Herbert Schöchl and colleagues compared two strategies for controlling bleeding in badly injured patients, in this 2011 analysis in Critical Care. One group, treated in Salzburg, received clotting-factor concentrates guided by a bedside test of clot strength, and no fresh frozen plasma. The other, drawn from a German trauma registry, received plasma-based care.

The groups had similar injury severity. Patients on the concentrate strategy needed far fewer donor blood products. Red-cell transfusion was avoided in nearly three in ten of them, against almost none in the plasma group. Platelet transfusion was avoided in the great majority. Death rates were similar between the strategies. The authors conclude that test-guided concentrates reduce exposure to donated blood products without harming survival.
europmc-pmc3220038:
Yan Zhang and colleagues tested blocking the immune checkpoint PD-L1 as a treatment for sepsis, in this 2010 mouse study in Critical Care. Sepsis can paralyze the immune system, partly through death of lymphocytes and failure of monocytes. The team induced sepsis in mice by puncturing the gut and measured checkpoint expression on immune cells a day later.

Septic mice carried more PD-1 and PD-L1 on their T cells, B cells, and monocytes than healthy controls. Giving an antibody that blocks PD-L1 significantly improved survival. Treated mice kept more of their lymphocytes, produced more of some inflammatory signals and less of a suppressive one, and cleared bacteria better. The authors propose PD-L1 blockade as a promising strategy against sepsis-driven immune suppression.
europmc-pmc3257638:
Asa Hakansson and Goran Molin reviewed the resident microbes of the human gut in relation to inflammation, in this 2011 article in Nutrients. The gut's microbial community can aggravate or calm inflammation, both locally and across the body, and probiotic products aim to tilt that balance. The authors restricted their evidence to human trials rather than cell or animal experiments.

They describe the dominant groups of organisms in the gastrointestinal tract and their inflammatory potential. Then they work through probiotic applications one by one. The list runs from whole-body immune modulation and liver injury to the metabolic syndrome, colorectal cancer, and inflammatory bowel disease. Radiation damage to the gut is covered too. A recurring caution concerns how much probiotic species and strains differ in their genes. The body can therefore respond very differently to each one. That point is often neglected when trial results are discussed.
europmc-pmc3376738:
Kondapalli and a large team reported in 2012 how the protein PINK1 switches on its partner Parkin, a process broken in some inherited Parkinson's disease. Faulty PINK1 genes cause a recessive, early form of the disease. The team tested whether PINK1 directly tags Parkin or fifteen other disease-linked proteins.

Only Parkin was tagged, at a single conserved spot, serine 65. Human PINK1 woke up when the voltage across mitochondrial membranes collapsed, and the tag it placed strongly boosted Parkin's enzyme activity. Blocking the spot or disabling PINK1 stopped the boost. Watching those tags could give the first readouts of this pathway in living tissue.
europmc-pmc3420138:
Deavall, Martin, Horner, and Roberts examined in 2012 how drugs can injure the body through oxidative stress. Reactive oxygen species arise from normal metabolism and double as signals, but cells must keep them leashed. When production outruns the antioxidant defenses, the overflow attacks DNA, proteins, and fats.

The review explains the kinds of damage these species inflict on key cell targets. It then gathers evidence tying them to real drug side effects: heart damage from the cancer drug doxorubicin, muscle wasting from an HIV drug, and hearing loss from cisplatin. Understanding which drugs tip the balance, the authors argue, should help design safer medicines and protect patients during treatment.
europmc-pmc3476838:
Vucenik and Stains reviewed the evidence linking obesity with cancer in a 2012 issue of the Annals journal of the New York Academy of Sciences. Obesity had already been tied to diabetes, heart disease, and high blood pressure. Population studies also link it to higher risk of several cancers, from colon and breast to liver and kidney, along with worse survival after diagnosis.

The authors survey how fat tissue might drive cancer: through growth signals, shifting energy balance, and steady low-level inflammation. One signaling cascade inside cells draws special attention as a shared hub and drug target. Vucenik and Stains close with practical advice. Keeping a healthy weight across life, they argue, ranks among the strongest steps a person can take against cancer.
europmc-pmc3503838: Species boundaries got an error warning. This 2012 paper shows tree-building error hurts species delimitation. The authors reveal the error. Their work guides taxonomy. Reid's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped species naming.
europmc-pmc3520838: CD19 got a B-cell biomarker review. This 2012 paper reviews CD19, a key B-cell marker for lymphoma care. The authors map the role. Their overview guides oncology. Wang's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped lymphoma therapy.
europmc-pmc3565338: Nanoparticles got a nature-plastic review. This 2013 paper reviews nature-plastic nanoparticles for drug delivery. The authors map the uses. Their review guides pharma. Nitta's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped nanomedicine. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3598338: Zebrafish got a brain-growth review. This 2013 paper reviews brain growth in zebrafish. The authors map the development. Their review guides biology. Schmidt's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped developmental biology. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3604638: Body ownership got a building-blocks study. This 2013 paper maps what builds the body-ownership illusion. The authors reveal the blocks. Their work guides neuroscience. Maselli's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped VR research.

fludd-philosophia-moysaica-1638:
Robert Fludd sums up his occult philosophy in Philosophia Moysaica, in Latin from 1638. Man mirrors the universe, the small world answering the great one in part by part. Moses himself is read as the first true philosopher of nature, whose words hide the secrets of creation for those with eyes to read them.

Weather, disease, and the elements all fall under Fludd's vast scheme. His famous engravings map soul, body, and cosmos in bold figures. Critics like Kepler and Gassendi crossed pens with him for years. The book forms the most elaborate summing up of Renaissance magic ever bound, a grand system built just as the new science rose.
frus-1861-d138:
Writing from Paris on 22 July 1861, William Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a last calm report. The dispatch is document 138 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dayton wrote the day after Bull Run, but the news had not yet reached Paris. His letter keeps the old mood for one more page. In the file it stands at the edge of a change that the next mails would bring in full. The mails that followed would bring the Bull Run tale in full and grim color. Grim color, when it came, would test the calm of every post in Europe.
frus-1861-d238:
News and judgment from James Shepherd Pike reached Seward's desk in a letter dated 14 June 1861. It was printed as Document 238 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It was written in the opening months of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d38:
Thomas Corwin wrote from Mexico City to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 June 1861. The dispatch is document 38 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Corwin spent 1861 trying to keep Mexico steady and friendly to the Union. Money, loans, and border fears filled his talks there. His end of June report shows an envoy working a hard post with few tools but his name and his voice. His post lacked money and troops, so words carried nearly the whole weight of his mission. Words, in Corwin's hands, had swayed crowds before; now they served a state.
frus-1862-d138:
Writing on 5 September 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 138 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d238:
William Stuart wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 September 1862, and the letter is printed as Document 238 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was running the British legation while Lord Lyons was absent.

Stuart wrote four days before Antietam, in the last stretch of the Maryland campaign's approach. The legation's letters home in this window helped London judge whether the invasion proved Southern staying power. This letter's date gives it its weight: it is a dispatch from the edge of the war's bloodiest day, written in ignorance of it. The British legation stood a short walk from the State Department, and messengers passed between them daily.
frus-1862-d338:
A Dayton report dated 23 October 1862 stands as Document 338 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

By late October, informed men in Paris could see the truce scheme failing for want of British support. Dayton's task shifted from warning to watching: would France act alone, or turn back to Mexico? His report that week belongs to the file's closing account of the autumn crisis, written as the tension drained away. Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d38:
Writing on 27 March 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 38 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The date falls in the winter of the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d438:
On 17 September 1862, the very day of the battle of Antietam, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Gabriel García Tassara. It is Document 438 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Business at the State Department went on even as the armies fought in Maryland, and notes to resident ministers were part of that day's work. Seward's dealings with Spain's minister covered the standing file between the two nations, from maritime questions to Mexico. Within days, Antietam and the emancipation order would change the tone of every foreign conversation in Washington. The note catches the Spanish exchange at the edge of that change, still in the forms of ordinary wartime routine.
frus-1862-d538:
Three days after the Dutch minister's note, on 22 July 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward replied to Roest van Limburg. The letter is Document 538 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Seward's July answers to resident ministers had to carry conviction in a discouraging month, and his Dutch reply was no exception. The substance between the governments remained the law and practice of the blockade as it touched Dutch trade. Van Limburg's legation was one of the steadiest in Washington. The correspondence shows no rupture. It shows only the friction natural between a blockading belligerent and a carrying neutral. The letter is a fair sample of that managed friction in the war's second summer.
frus-1862-d638:
On 2 July 1861 Townsend Harris dispatched this letter from Japan to the Secretary of State. It is Document 638 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Harris wrote days before the first battle of Bull Run, in ignorance of it that would last for months. His Japan letters in this period report the grinding detail of a new treaty relationship. They cover audiences and disputes over the ports. They also cover the shogun's government's own troubles with foreigners. The contrast inside the volume is striking. Ministers in Europe reported a war for the Union's life. Harris, at the far end of the earth, reported whether the treaty of 1858 would hold. Both were the same government's business.
frus-1863p1-d138:
A month-end pair for London opens with this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, dated 31 March 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 138 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward's month-end pair closed his March file for London. The brief he fed Adams had not changed its heart all spring: hold Britain fair, stop the ships, keep the tone firm but cool. This letter opens the pair of 31 March. It is the kind of sheet that kept the long game in play, one steamer at a time.
frus-1863p1-d238:
Reporting on 16 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is document 238 in the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

The CSS Alabama, built in a British yard, had escaped to sea in 1862 and was burning Union merchant ships. London's handling of such ships hung over every report Adams sent home. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d338:
On 12 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward put the American position in writing to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. This note is document 338 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

For historians, this exchange shows Anglo-American tension being managed day by day. It is the paper record of a war that never happened between the two countries. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d38: Marked private and confidential, this paper is dated 11 September 1862. It is printed as document 38 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It sits among the Confederate letters in that part of the volume. The evidence gives its mark and date but no writer and no name addressed, so this note claims no more than that.
frus-1863p1-d438:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 2 April 1863 letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d538:
In the flow of wartime mail, Lord Lyons wrote to William H. Seward on 27 May 1863. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d638:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London sent an official note to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State on 16 October 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d138: Kirk wrote to the Secretary of State again on November 18, 1943, his second Cairo dispatch in two days in this series. It is Document 138 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The quickening pace of the host's reports matches the nearness of the conference, which opened on November 22. The record gives the parties and the date and no subject. The dispatch rests in the Foreign Relations volume.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d238:
Minutes record President Roosevelt's second meeting with the Joint Chiefs of Staff aboard the Iowa, on 19 November 1943 in the admiral's cabin. At some thirty-five thousand characters, the record is long, and its printed opening turns on the fight over a single commander for the war in Europe.

Roosevelt says he likes proposal A, the unified command plan, dislikes proposal B. He will take the matter up with Churchill at the first chance, though a compromise may follow. Admiral King calls A plain logic; General Marshall attacks committee command, citing a year and a half of failure in the Middle East. The chiefs then count forces: some eleven million Americans and four and a half million British in uniform by January, with American strength in England already matching the British.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d338:
Secretary of War Henry Stimson sent John McCloy an eyes-only telegram from Washington on 28 November 1943, numbered 1124. It answers McCloy's reports from Cairo on the civil affairs negotiation with Foreign Secretary Eden.

Stimson says he and Secretary Hull agree with the key suggestion. The European Advisory Commission's draft recommendations should go to the Combined Chiefs of Staff for comment. That step should come before any final submission to governments. Both men welcome Eden's tentative agreement to drop the pressure for moving the Combined Civil Affairs Committee to London. The State Department, he adds, thinks the proposed British-American commission on the French political situation should sit in London. Stimson closes by congratulating McCloy heartily on working out so satisfactory a solution.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d38: A second message from Churchill to Roosevelt is also dated October 5, 1943, and it follows as Document 38 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The prime minister often split his business into separate notes rather than one long letter. Which errand this one ran, the record does not say. It is preserved in the Foreign Relations series, in the dense October traffic before the Moscow Conference opened.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d438:
December 4, 1943 was the opening day of the Second Cairo Conference, and the Combined Chiefs of Staff, the joint American-British military command, held a formal session that day. The minutes printed here come from the State Department's published record of the Cairo and Tehran conferences, where the chiefs' meetings sit alongside the talks of Roosevelt and Churchill.

A reader gets the working level of the alliance: senior officers weighing operations, shipping, and manpower, and recording the points they agreed on. Because the second Cairo meeting had to finish what Tehran started, these sessions matter. They show strategy being fixed in detail while the political leaders met in the same city.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d538:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull set out this memorandum on January 3, 1944, as the government in Washington took stock after the Tehran and Cairo conferences. Hull had not traveled to the summits, yet his department had to make their results work. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Departmental memoranda by the Secretary gathered a subject into one considered paper, rather than a hasty cable. Hull was then the administration's elder statesman of diplomacy, architect of its trade policy and a planner of the postwar order. For readers, the memorandum shows the Secretary thinking on paper at the opening of the decisive year.
frus-1944-quebec-d138:
American policy toward Hungary, as State Department planners stated it for Quebec in September 1944, began from frustration. Hungary had repeatedly said it wanted out of the war but had taken no realistic step. Budapest hoped the Anglo-Americans would protect it from Soviet Russia, and it clung to territories gained with German help.

Draft armistice terms had already gone to the European Advisory Commission. The paper rules out American troops in Hungary's occupation, but wants political representatives there after surrender. Long term, Washington favored a broadly based provisional government, land and electoral reform, and frontiers starting from the pre-Munich lines. Ethnic adjustments were possible, including a small strip of Transylvania returning to Hungary.
frus-1944-quebec-d238:
Taylor cabled urgently from Vatican City on September 11, 1944, about Italian relief shipments. His greatest concern was that material accumulated in America for the Italian relief committee would not reach Italy because of failures to ship on schedule. The first shipment should already have arrived, and failure to deliver would badly damage American prestige.

His remedy was simple and practical. Allocate one or two ships to strictly relief voyages, with standard cargoes of staples and essentials, kept constantly en route between an American port and convenient Italian ports. Dedicated ships would avoid the delays and complications of mixed cargoes of munitions and other goods. The people in distress, Taylor wrote, do not understand shipping difficulties.
frus-1944-quebec-d38:
A second Roosevelt message to Churchill is dated August 30, 1944. The State Department printed both messages that day. They appear in the pre-conference correspondence of the Quebec 1944 volume.

Paired messages before a summit usually split the business. Some points could be settled by letter. Others needed a room and a handshake. August 1944 left plenty in both piles. For readers, this companion message completes a day's preparation. The two leaders had written to each other for four years. They were about to meet again on Canadian soil. It would be their second conference there. The letters show how much business they handled in writing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d138:
Minutes of the first meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board are dated 4 February 1946. The advisory board gathered the departments' intelligence chiefs under the new director. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

First meetings matter: they seat the members, fix the habits, and test whether rivals can sit in one room under a chairman not their own. The advisory board was the January design's working level, where the services' chiefs advised the director of central intelligence. Readers can watch the experiment begin here. The men in that room had spent the autumn fighting over the system's shape. Now they had to run it together. The minutes show how the running started.
frus-1945-50-intel-d238:
A memorandum dated 11 January 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The reader was Acting Secretary of State Lovett. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 238, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The Dulles survey team was checking how well the CIA worked, and agencies across Washington were stating their views on the record.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d338:
The Secretary of Defense’s Special Assistant (McNeil) addressed a letter to Mathias F. Correa on 2 February 1948. Readers meet it as document 338 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

Senior men used letters to make requests that could not be brushed aside, since the paper itself proved the ask. Its worth now is the voice: a chief stating his case as he wished it to be read. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d38:
Harold Smith, director of the Bureau of the Budget, wrote to President Truman on 31 October 1945. Smith was the president's chief adviser on the machinery of government. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

When the budget director wrote to the president, the subject had reached decision level. Smith had strong views on how intelligence should be organized, favoring a modest central staff over a grand new agency. His memorandum put that view where it counted most. Readers should mark this paper: the plans that finally emerged in January bear the stamp of the Budget Bureau's thinking. Smith's letters to Truman are where that stamp was pressed into the record.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d138:
General Macready, head of the army side of the British Staff Mission in Washington, wrote to Assistant Secretary of War McCloy on 20 January 1945. His letter, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, is headed “Bremen Enclave.” It moves the ports dispute close to settlement.

The British Chiefs of Staff, Macready reports, are ready to accept the formula worked out at the War Department on 5 January. They ask the American chiefs to confirm their reading of one or two points. He attaches the formula with two small amendments underlined, so both sides read it the same way. One amendment pins down the role of a deputy controller, an officer who runs only his own office's agents inside another power's zone.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d238:
Persia belongs on the conference table, Churchill told Roosevelt on 15 January 1945. His top secret message, number 890, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. He proposes discussion with Stalin, or between the foreign secretaries, and he quotes the pledge all three signed at Tehran.

That declaration of December 1943 records the three governments as at one with Iran in desiring her independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity. Recent Russian conduct in Persia, Churchill argues, departs from those words. Moscow refused to accept Persia's decision to grant no concessions until after the war. Its pressure brought down a prime minister who would not grant the oil demands at once. The new premier, backed by parliament, holds the same line.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d338: Harry Hopkins coached from the sidelines at Yalta with short handwritten notes passed to the President. This one, dated February 5, 1945, concerns the breaking up of Germany. Hopkins urged Roosevelt to call the matter very important and urgent. The three foreign ministers, he wrote, should bring in a proposal the next day. It would set a method for reaching a decision on dismemberment at an early date. The slip shows the adviser feeding words to the President mid-session.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d38: Churchill opened the new year with a message to Roosevelt on 1 January 1945. It is document 38 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta, published by the Department of State. January was departure month for both delegations, so the tone of the correspondence shifted from general planning toward the practical business of travel and meeting arrangements.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d438:
What still needs settling fills this delegation checklist of February 10, 1945. Poland probably need not be discussed before the plenary, it says. The Declaration on Liberated Europe stands in the same state. On Iran, the British may propose adopting their paper, and Matthews holds a copy.

On reparations, the British had not yet agreed to the Soviet-American paper. Eden, the memo notes, wants three things: Hungarian control rules extended to Bulgaria, Bulgarian reparations for Greece, and a statement against a Russian-backed Tito-Bulgaria alliance. The paper, likely prepared by Hiss for Stettinius, is a crib sheet for the conference's penultimate day.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d138:
Ambassador Winant asked for instructions on press arrangements in an urgent telegram from London on July 13, 1945. The message is document 138 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. London correspondents had heard from their Washington offices that a meeting place would be fixed for reporters late in the conference.

The correspondents claimed they would be told a time and place where they could join the President's party, and that the embassy in London would notify them. Winant reports that the embassy has no record of any instructions on the point. He asks Washington to tell him how to handle such inquiries. The query shows the loose end left by the press ban: reporters were shut out of Potsdam, but nobody had yet told them where to wait for the end.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d238:
Ambassador Kirk reported a split in Rome's cabinet over the war declaration in a telegram dated July 9, 1945. The message is document 238 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Kirk had seen Renato Prunas, the Italian foreign ministry's secretary general, the evening before.

After Washington's approval arrived, Prunas said, the Council of Ministers met. Most ministers, including the Socialists, favored immediate and active participation against Japan. Only the Communists were cool, insisting any Italian part in the Far East war be symbolic rather than actual. With timing and degree in dispute, Rome asked Washington when the declaration should come. Kirk repeated the Department's line: the choice was Italy's, but the sooner the better. Reports from Moscow suggested the Soviets did not look favorably on the move.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d338:
Robert Murphy, the political adviser in Germany, objected on June 27, 1945, to the shape of the French occupation zone. In an extract of his cable from Hoechst, he regretted the pressure on France to accept southern Württemberg against its wishes. The grant, he said, split an old German state and might wipe it out as a political unit.

Württemberg, Murphy noted, had a long liberal history. He added that Ambassador Winant and Mr. Mosely had also objected. Forcing the division clashed, he argued, with the allied aim of breaking up the Reich by reviving its traditional states, Prussia aside. Zone lines, his cable warns, could do lasting political harm.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d38: Truman gave Hopkins his answer for Stalin in this telegram of May 28, 1945. Two of Hopkins's messages had been received. Hopkins might inform Stalin that the President saw no objection to meeting in the Berlin area. About the 15th of July appeared to be a practicable date for him. The wire, sent by Navy channels through the naval attaché in Moscow, reached Hopkins while his Kremlin talks still ran. Its lines fixed the frame of the Potsdam Conference — place and month — weeks before the leaders traveled.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d438:
Klieforth, the American chargé in Prague, cabled on June 28, 1945, that one issue towers over Czechoslovakia's reconstruction: the minority problem. Its solution, he writes, means the transfer to Germany and Hungary of about three million citizens, a fifth of the country's population. A second phase would replace them with about as many Czechoslovaks, most of them uprooted in turn.

Together, transfer and replacement would touch forty percent of the population. Prague knows the transfers need allied agreement, Klieforth reports, but the earliest possible agreement is essential, since all reconstruction is makeshift until then. He ends with a warning: delay could feed a dramatic leader, backed by radicals, seeking a solution by force.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d538:
Second-year lend-lease for Britain is anticipated in a briefing book paper dated July 6, 1945. Churchill may seek a commitment, at least in principle, it warns. The commitment would fix the amount of lend-lease for the United Kingdom and the British Commonwealth. It would cover the second year of Phase II. The existing agreement covers the first year, applied to calendar 1945.

At Quebec in 1944, the paper recalls, Churchill sought Roosevelt's agreement in principle. He obtained it: 6.5 billion dollars of lend-lease during the first year of Phase II. The American Joint Chiefs had not considered that the Pacific war's needs called for anything near that amount. No corresponding benefit to the United States was requested in return. Later Washington talks settled on 5.5 billion dollars in total.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d638:
George Wadsworth, the U.S. minister in Lebanon, sent a detailed confidential report from Beirut on June 30, 1945. It is document 638 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Its subject is the Troupes Speciales, the local forces officered by France in Syria and Lebanon.

Wadsworth gives a careful head count, checked with local ministers and British staff men. Before the May troubles the force stood near 20,000 men, some 5,000 in Lebanon and 15,000 in Syria. About 5,500 Syrians had since deserted, while the Lebanese ranks held firm. The 9,000 Syrian troops left stayed under French officers but under close British control. Wadsworth lists where they were held, from camps in the Bekaa valley to barracks at Aleppo and Mezze airport.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1038:
The European Advisory Commission sent this report to the four occupying governments on July 25, 1945. It transmits an agreement on certain additional requirements to be imposed upon Germany. The June 5 declaration on Germany's defeat had promised such added political, economic, and military demands. The commission urges the four governments to approve the agreement and pass it to the Allied representatives in Berlin.

The report attaches comments on single clauses. When conditions allow, all German research on war or war material should be flatly abolished by public order. German authorities should also hand over the plates and tools used to print money tokens for lands Germany once occupied. Further comments guard the property of other nations held in Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1138:
Ambassador Winant wrote from London once more on 24 July 1945. His cables came near daily during the Potsdam weeks. Each tracked British official thinking as the summit's choices took shape in Germany.

Reports from London added texture that the conference room could not give. Winant heard party talk, press views, and Whitehall's private mood. Washington used that stream to judge its ally's stands and staying power. This dispatch keeps the embassy's close watch going into the summit's second week. It is a small part of a large, steady flow of London reporting.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1238:
The Acting Secretary of State set down this memorandum on 17 July 1945, the day the conference opened. Grew's notes from Washington fixed the home office's thinking on paper. Staff memoranda did the quiet reasoning that leaders later turned into choices.

A memorandum from the man running the department carried weight beyond its length. It could frame a question, record a call, or set a line for the desks below. This one dates from the summit's first day, when Washington's part in the talks was just taking shape. It is the home office thinking aloud, in its chief's hand.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1338:
On 18 July 1945, George Allen wrote to Loy Henderson, the director of the Office of Near Eastern and African Affairs. Allen was Henderson's deputy, so the paper moved inside a single office of the State Department. It dates from the second day of the Potsdam Conference, where Truman, Churchill, and Stalin met outside Berlin in July and August 1945.

Inside-office papers show how a bureau shaped its advice before it reached the secretary of state. Henderson's office covered a wide map, from Iran and the Arab lands to Africa, at a time when all of it was in flux. The message helps readers trace how American policy for that region was built, step by step, by the men assigned to it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-138:
State Department minutes record a meeting of July 30, 1945, as Potsdam moved toward its close. The formal minute sets give the conference its ordered skeleton. This one joined the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States. It covers business done two days before the final protocol was signed.

Readers find the session's work stated cleanly: topics, speakers, outcomes. In the last days the minutes grow dense with decisions. They show the machinery of agreement running at full speed. Paired with the note-takers' drafts, the formal minutes let readers judge how the record itself was built.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-38:
One line in volume two of the Potsdam papers states that no record of a meeting's substance has been found. It is the thirty-eighth unnumbered item following document 710, sitting between the records of July 20, 1945. The meeting it concerns is not even named in the line itself.

Such notes are the editors' way of keeping the record honest. Rather than pass over a known meeting in silence, they mark the gap in print. The reader is told that the conference's paper trail breaks at this point. Whatever was said, and whatever it may have moved, cannot be recovered from the files the editors searched. The entry belongs to a family of like notes throughout this volume. Together they map how much of the Potsdam Conference was transacted off the record, in talks no secretary minuted.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d738:
A second Yost memorandum bears the date August 9, 1945, as document 738. The Central Secretariat's executive secretary had more than one thread to close. Two memos in a day mirror the secretariat's load. This one joined the post-conference papers of the second Potsdam volume.

Paired wrap-up memos show the range of loose ends. Texts, records, and duties all needed owners after the close. Yost assigned them in writing. Readers see the unglamorous labor that makes a clean archive. The document also marks how long Potsdam's shadow ran: a week on, its staff still worked its files.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d838:
Kennan wrote again from Moscow on July 18, 1945, in document 838. The chargé sent a second letter in two days to the Acting Secretary of State. His reports fed Washington while Harriman sat at Potsdam. This one was printed in the second Potsdam volume beside the first.

Two letters in two days show an embassy with much to report. Moscow watched the summit and reacted in ways worth cabling. Readers follow Kennan's reading of those reactions. The document extends one of the volume's most literate threads. His dispatches from this summer are still quoted, and letters like this one show why.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d938:
The Acting Secretary of State cabled Edwin Pauley on July 26, 1945, about a British memorandum on Soviet reparation claims. The British foresaw a chance that single Soviet republics might file separate claims. They also imagined republics seeking their own seats on a reparations commission.

London's view was to resist most such claims. White Russia and the Ukraine could be heard, by the San Francisco precedent, but their shares must come out of the Soviet total. Baltic state claims should not be entertained at all. Washington's reply called any policy premature. No sign yet showed whether Moscow would raise the questions.
frus-1952-54v16-d1038: The final declaration on Indochina from the 1954 Geneva Conference in FRUS. Vietnam was temporarily divided. This entry preserves that declaration. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
frus-1969-76v10-d238: A 1969-1976 FRUS backchannel message on Vietnam. The secret channel. This document preserves that message. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298438: United Medical Systems-DE took its September 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Medical deals get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298838: Smiths Detection doubled its December 2006 protest — two case numbers, one detection-tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299338: Vaden Industries took its March 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the call on the claims. The firm challenged the award, and the ruling tests the protest in full. The bid-law hearing treats every challenger alike. The process stays the same for all.
gao-gaoreports-b-299738: Camnetics Mfg. took its June 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The manufacturer said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the claims. Factory-floor contracts get the same fair-play ruling as high-tech deals.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-238: Drug offenders' benefit denials had limited impact in 2005, and GAO's report says various factors might limit the effects of the denial laws. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the punishment's bite deserved honest assessment. The factors had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-438: The LOCAL TV Act's admin funds looked done in 2005, and GAO's report says the money may no longer be necessary. The review gives the quiet verdict. The program's paperwork was paid up. The funds were no longer needed. The program's paperwork was paid up.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-538: Global trade talks were back on track in 2005, and GAO's report says the WTO negotiations progressed, though considerable work remained. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the ambitious goals deserved honest effort. The work had to continue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-238: Contractors with Social Security numbers needed stronger protections in 2006, and GAO's report says safeguards were required when vendors held SSNs. The findings demand the locks. The report warns that the nine-digit keys deserved guarding. The protections had to be stronger.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-338: States' 911 wireless funds got a GAO review in 2006, and the report examines collection and use of the enhanced 911 money. The findings follow the dollars. The report warns that the emergency-call funds should save lives, not budgets. The funds had to be used right.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-438: Privatized military housing needed attention in 2006, and GAO's report says management issues required focus as the program matured. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the troops' homes deserved good landlords. The issues had to be addressed. The troops deserved good landlords.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-538: The Pentagon's EEO pilot needed a better evaluation in 2006, and GAO's report says the program was underway, though the evaluation plan needed improvement. The findings balance the start and the gaps. The report warns that the fairness experiment deserved real measurement. The plan had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-638: Export controls for dual-use tech needed fixing in 2006, and GAO's report says Commerce's system needed improvements to protect U.S. interests. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the civilian-military tech should not leak. The system had to be tightened.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-938: The Pentagon's mobility study had holes in 2006, and GAO's report says the limitations raised questions about the capability assessment. The findings doubt the conclusions. The report warns that the lift capacity for war needed honest math. The study had to be solid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-138: The State Department's watchdog got watched in 2007, and GAO's report examines what the department's inspector general actually accomplished all year. The findings audit the auditor in careful detail, grading its cases and its reach. The report's meta-lesson stands firm: even the watchdogs need watching, and the diplomats' overseer was no exception.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-238: Health IT was racing ahead of privacy in 2007, and GAO's report says a comprehensive privacy approach was needed for the national strategy. The findings demand the safeguards. The report warns that the digital chart should not become a public record. The patients' secrets needed locks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-38: Small-business research grants needed better tracking in 2007, and GAO's report says agencies had to strengthen their data on the innovation program. The findings demand the numbers. The report warns that the seed money for inventors needed sunlight. The data had to be solid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-538: The Pentagon's computer buying needed grown-up rules in 2007 — GAO's report says the department had to fully spell out how it managed tech investments. The findings demand the written playbook. The report's refrain: billion-dollar systems deserve better than improvisation.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1138: The Government Accountability Office dug into health Information Technology: HHS Has Taken Important Steps to Address Privacy Principles and Challenges, Although More Work Remains in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-38: Covering the 2007 tax filing season, this Government Accountability Office report finds the IRS continuing a trend of improvement in processing returns. It also urges the agency to evaluate ways to cut costs and boost voluntary tax compliance. The review balances praise for smoother operations with pressure to do more with less, as the IRS handles hundreds of millions of returns each year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-538: GAO published its findings on supply Chain Security: CBP Works with International Entities to Promote Global Customs Security Standards and Initiatives, but Challenges Remain in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
godwin-man-in-the-moone-1638:
Francis Godwin wrote The Man in the Moone in the last years of his life. The tale came out in 1638, after his death. Its hero, Domingo Gonsales, is a Spaniard who flees a duel and roams the world. In the isle of St. Helena he trains wild geese to bear him in the air.

The geese bear him up past Earth to the Moon on their yearly flight. He finds the Moon a green land of tall folk who live in peace. Their tongue is tones, not words, and he learns it in part. The tale is a root text of the trip to the Moon.
grimke-letters-equality-sexes-1838:
Sarah Grimké published Letters on the Equality of the Sexes, and the Condition of Woman in 1838 in Boston. Grimké, a South Carolina abolitionist who had left a slaveholding family, wrote the letters first for a newspaper. Speaking tours by her and her sister had drawn attacks on women who spoke in public.

Grimké answered from the Bible itself, arguing that scripture grants woman equality and that men had twisted it to rule her. She surveyed women's condition across lands and demanded equal education and rights. The letters linked the abolitionist and feminist causes at their joint birth. They stand as a founding document of American feminism, bold for their time and place.
