Wildschut and colleagues show that circuit dilution is not the whole story, and that kidney function can dominate dosing in these fragile patients.
plos-pone-0011038:
Dawn Thompson, Lene Martini and Jennifer Whistler published this cocaine study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Addictive drugs raise brain dopamine, and chronic use selectively lowers the D2 dopamine receptor, tipping the balance of signaling toward the D1 receptor. What removes D2 receptors in the living brain was unknown, so the authors studied mice lacking a sorting protein called GASP-1.

Comparing normal and knockout mice during cocaine sensitization, the process where repeated doses produce growing responses, they tied the D2 loss to receptor sorting after activation. Lowering D2 or raising D1 signaling each shifted the receptor ratio the same way chronic cocaine does. Thompson and colleagues identify a molecular route by which repeated drug exposure rewires dopamine balance. That route is a candidate target for treatments aimed at the receptor loss itself, not just dopamine levels.
plos-pone-0011138:
Senapathy, Bhasi, Mattox and colleagues presented a gene reading method in PLOS ONE in 2010. Reading a whole genome costs time and money, and much of the DNA does not code for proteins. The authors described a way to pull out only the useful regions before sequencing.

Their targeted method enriches the parts of the genome most likely to matter for function. That focus makes gene reading cheaper and sharper for many studies. Labs hunting disease genes could screen more people for the same cost. The approach helps turn raw sequence data into findings that can be used.
plos-pone-0011238:
Glauche, Herberg and Roeder modeled stem cell variation in PLOS ONE in 2010. Embryonic stem cells vary in levels of a protein called Nanog, which helps keep them able to become any cell type. The authors used a math model to ask how that wavering affects the cell population.

The model shows noise in one protein can keep a population flexible rather than locked in. Some cells drift toward change while others stay ready to revert. That insight helps labs control stem cells for regenerative medicine. It reframes randomness not as a flaw but as part of how stem cells keep their options open.
plos-pone-0011338:
Ivan Laponogov and co-authors reported in 2010 on enzymes that cut and reseal DNA. These enzymes untangle DNA by slicing both strands of one segment, letting another segment pass through the gap, then sealing the break. The cycle is vital for copying and reading DNA, and many cancer and infection drugs target it.

Using detailed structural work, the team captured how the enzyme holds the cut segment and how the break is made and then closed. The pictures explain how the enzyme keeps a dangerous break under tight control instead of letting broken DNA loose in the cell. That control is exactly what some drugs exploit to kill cancer cells. A clearer structure helps chemists design drugs that jam the enzyme at the right moment.
plos-pone-0011438:
Abdel-Majid Khatib and co-authors followed a growth factor during zebrafish fin regrowth in 2010. Zebrafish regrow amputated fins quickly, and the factor VEGF-C helps guide that rebuilding. The factor is first made as a longer raw form that must be cut to become active, and the team tracked both forms during regeneration.

They found the uncut raw form does not merely wait its turn; it actively blocks regeneration. The same molecule thus promotes growth in one form and brakes it in another. That built-in brake may keep regrowth orderly, preventing the fin from overshooting its proper shape. For regenerative medicine, the lesson is that delivering a growth factor is not enough. Its processing state decides whether it helps or hinders, a subtlety any future therapy must respect.
plos-pone-0011538:
Thomas Chertemps and co-authors showed in 2010 that one mosquito protein shapes malaria parasite development at two separate checkpoints. To spread, Plasmodium parasites must cross the mosquito's gut wall and later invade its salivary glands, the two tightest squeezes of their journey. The team studied a protein of the mosquito Anopheles gambiae called PRS1 and its effect at both steps.

Modulating PRS1 changed how well parasites developed at the midgut step and again at the salivary gland step. A single mosquito-side handle on both bottlenecks is a valuable find, since most control ideas target only one stage. Blocking the parasite inside the mosquito stops transmission before any human is bitten. Such transmission-blocking strategies are a growing hope for malaria control, and a double checkpoint protein is exactly the kind of target they need.
plos-pone-0011638:
Silvio Brugger and colleagues tracked pneumococcal bacteria in children's noses around a vaccine launch, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Children often carry more than one strain of Streptococcus pneumoniae at once. Such mixed carriage lets strains swap genes, which can change their capsules and spread drug resistance.

The team compared mixed carriage before and after the seven-strain conjugate vaccine arrived. Their tracking shows how vaccination reshaped the whole carried community, not just the targeted strains. That fuller picture helps officials anticipate replacement strains early and keep vaccine programmes effective over time.
plos-pone-0011738:
Kristin Stieler and Nicole Fischer tested a human defence protein against the retrovirus XMRV, in PLOS ONE in 2010. At the time, XMRV was thought to play a part in two human illnesses, prostate cancer and chronic fatigue syndrome. Beyond those disease links, its tissue targets and its response to the body's anti-retroviral factors needed study.

The authors showed the protein APOBEC3G sharply cuts the virus's power to infect new cells. That result adds XMRV to the list of retroviruses this defender can blunt. It also sharpens a tool for studying how such factors might be used against retroviral infection more broadly.
plos-pone-0011838:
Nadia Innamorato and colleagues asked in 2010 why some brains suffer more from a Parkinson's-like toxin than others. They worked with MPTP, a chemical that harms the dopamine-making nerve cells lost in Parkinson's disease. Their focus was Nrf2, a master switch for antioxidant defenses, and heme oxygenase-1, one of the protective genes it turns on.

Comparing normal mice with mice missing Nrf2 or missing the oxygenase gene showed that the two losses do not carry the same risk. The pattern separates the broad protection run by Nrf2 from the narrower role of a single gene under it. Knowing which layer of defense matters most could guide attempts to shield dopamine cells from toxic damage.
plos-pone-0011938:
Chadwick Rittenhouse and colleagues warned in 2010 that forest bird conservation may be grading itself against a moving target. Counting bird diversity year by year can miss slow, steady change. When each generation accepts the current community as normal, the baseline itself shifts and decline hides in plain sight.

Comparing forest bird community structure across longer spans, the team found evidence of exactly that shifting baseline. Their result argues for judging today's forests against historical records, not against last decade's counts. For conservation planning, the distinction matters: a forest can look stable in annual reports while quietly losing the character it held a lifetime ago.
plos-pone-0012038:
Nadine Rohwer and co-workers showed in 2010 how low oxygen inside a stomach tumor decides how well chemotherapy works. Solid tumors often outgrow their blood supply and turn hypoxic, and hypoxic cells resist drugs, a central obstacle in oncology. The oxygen sensor HIF-1α had been linked to that resistance.

The team found HIF-1α determining gastric cancer chemosensitivity by modulating two major control proteins, p53 and NF-κB. Naming the middlemen matters: blocking the sensor alone may be hard, while its downstream partners offer other points of attack. The work supports pairing chemotherapy with treatments that break the low-oxygen defense.
plos-pone-0012138:
Jonathan Bohbot and Joseph Dickens studied how insect repellents work on mosquito noses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Familiar repellents, from DEET to picaridin, keep mosquitoes from biting people, yet scientists argued for years about how they actually work. Some theories said the chemicals jam the insect's sense of smell; others said mosquitoes simply hate the smell itself.

The authors tested how these repellents act on the odor receptors in mosquito antennae. They found the chemicals modulate those receptors, changing how the mosquito reads the scents around it, including human odor. Pinning down the mechanism helps chemists design better repellents on purpose instead of by trial and error, a real gain against mosquito-borne disease.
plos-pone-0012238:
Malin Johansson, Jenny Gustafsson, Karolina Sjöberg, and co-authors watched bacteria breach the colon's defenses in PLOS ONE in 2010. The colon holds an enormous bacterial population inches from the body's own tissue, kept apart by an inner mucus layer that is normally sterile. In a standard mouse model of colitis, the team asked whether bacteria cross that inner layer before inflammation begins or only after it.

They found bacteria penetrating the inner mucus before visible inflammation starts. That ordering matters: the breach may be a cause of the flare, not just its wreckage. If so, shoring up the mucus barrier becomes a treatment strategy for ulcerative colitis, beside the usual approach of damping the immune response.
plos-pone-0012338:
Jason Popesku, Christopher Martyniuk, Nancy Denslow, and co-authors watched a fish brain center answer dopamine, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dopamine is a master regulator of reproduction across vertebrates, acting on the hypothalamus, the brain's hormone command center. The team built a method to compare, in the same living experiment, both the gene messages and the proteins of that tissue as dopamine acts.

Messages and proteins do not always move together, so reading both shows where control really sits. Reproduction timing in fish governs aquaculture breeding and wild population responses to pollution. A method that fuses the two readouts can be reused for any hormone and any tissue, well beyond this study.
plos-pone-0012438:
Esther Herrmann, Brian Hare, Josep Call and fellow researchers compared thinking skills in bonobos and chimpanzees, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. The two apes are close kin and share much of their behavior, yet they differ in key ways. Bonobos tend to be more careful and more at ease with others, while chimps compete more boldly.

The team ran both species through the same set of mental tests. Each ape did better on some tasks: bonobos shone in certain social tests, and chimps in some tool and space tasks. Fair side-by-side tests like these show how mood, social style, and mind may have grown up together. They also help trace the roots of human thought, since both apes are close kin to us as well.
plos-pone-0012538:
Giuseppe Astarita, Kwang-Mook Jung, Nicole Berchtold and colleagues measured a key brain fat in the livers of Alzheimer's patients, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. DHA, an omega-3 fat, protects and nourishes brain cells, and brain levels fall in Alzheimer's disease alongside memory. Whether the liver — the body's fat-processing hub — fails to supply enough was the question.

Liver DHA production was deficient, and the shortfall correlated with cognitive impairment in patients. A liver-to-brain supply failure reframes part of Alzheimer's as a whole-body metabolic problem. It suggests dietary or liver-targeted strategies deserve testing alongside brain-focused drugs.
plos-pone-0012638:
Karn, Young and Laukaitis studied a smell gene that may keep two mouse types from mating with each other. The house mouse splits into two subspecies that meet in parts of Europe. Crosses can yield unfit young, so choosing a mate from one's own group protects future offspring.

Their 2010 paper reports that a vomeronasal receptor gene, used in smell, carries different fixed versions in each subspecies. A smell cue tied to group identity could steer mating choice. The case shows how new species can begin to form while groups still live side by side.
plos-pone-0012738:
Sun, He, Hou and co-authors followed a motor protein through sperm formation in the Chinese mitten crab. This crab's sperm has no tail and a round shape, quite unlike most animal sperm. Building its cap, the acrosome, and reshaping its nucleus need careful internal transport.

Their 2010 study places the motor protein myosin Va at both jobs. Motors that carry cargo inside cells are ancient, so finding one shaping crab sperm links crab biology to a wide field. The work also informs crab breeding in aquaculture.  Sperm form varies hugely across crustaceans, making each case instructive.
plos-pone-0012838:
Kraatz, Meng, Weksler and co-authors traced how teeth evolved in rabbits, hares and their kin. These animals, the Duplicidentata, have highly specialised teeth far from their ancestors' pattern. That specialisation long confused efforts to match their tooth cusps with those of other mammals.

Their 2010 study found a new trend in how premolars turn molar-like across this group. Set patterns in tooth change help palaeontologists read fossils and place extinct forms. Teeth are often the only fossils left, so their rules carry real weight.  Fossil and living forms were compared across the whole group.
plos-pone-0317638:
Geoffroy Vellieux and four co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One study. It is an attempt to create a rat model of Lance-Adams syndrome. This severe jerking disorder can follow oxygen loss to the brain. No good animal model exists, which blocks research into how the condition works. The team tried three procedures that lowered or removed oxygen in sedated rats. Each rat was then revived and watched daily for jerks.

None of the three procedures produced the jerking the team sought. This held even though many animals survived the oxygen loss. The authors publish these negative results openly. They argue the procedures still need refinement. A faithful model would be a precious tool for testing treatments. This record helps the next team avoid the same dead ends.
plos-pone-0331638:
Koichiro Ito and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One imaging study on seeing egg follicles deep inside ovarian tissue without cutting it open. Doctors freeze ovarian tissue to preserve fertility for young cancer patients, and knowing where follicles sit would help assess that tissue. Ordinary optical coherence microscopy struggles with grainy speckle noise at depth, so the team added speckle modulation to a near-infrared system.

In mouse ovaries the method clearly showed the youngest follicles near the surface and more developed ones in older tissue. In ovarian samples from two teenage leukemia patients, it revealed follicle structures several hundred micrometers deep, matching stained sections. The authors call it a feasibility step toward noninvasive checks of tissue saved for fertility preservation.
plos-pone-0334638:
Bo van Engelen and colleagues asked whether making primary schools healthier also makes children learn better. The Dutch program they studied serves healthy lunches and runs structured activity sessions during the school day. Earlier work had shown gains in children's health, but effects on school subjects were unclear, so the team followed eight schools for four years using national tests.

Children in schools running the full program, with both lunches and activity, improved in mathematics far more than children in control schools, and the gap grew over time. Activity-only schools gained less in math. Reading improved a little in the first year at full-program schools but faded by year four, while activity-only schools kept small reading gains. The results favor the combined approach.
plos-pone-0334738:
Diego Alexander Garzón-Alvarado led a team of four authors modeling how emotions spread between people, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Moods are contagious: a calm or anxious person shifts those nearby. The team built a dynamical systems model in which emotions couple like oscillators, using the circumplex map of affect that places feelings on axes of pleasantness and arousal.

Garzón-Alvarado's equations show how moods can synchronize between individuals, falling into step like coupled rhythms. A formal model lets researchers test ideas about crowds, teams, and online contagion that talk alone cannot settle. It also suggests when a group tips from mixed moods into one shared state. Such models may one day guide how schools and workplaces handle emotional climates.
plos-pone-0344038:
Mahnaz Sanjari and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One analysis of three painful joint and back conditions in Iran, using Global Burden of Disease data from 1990 to 2019. Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, together with pain in the lower back, are leading causes of years lived with disability. The team tracked incidence and prevalence nationally and by province, along with the risk factors driving each condition.

Total case numbers for all three climbed over the three decades. Rates of osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis rose even after adjusting for age, while low back pain rates eased somewhat. Women bore more of the two arthritis conditions, men more back pain, and each condition peaked in a different age band. The authors urge prompt policies and better-directed resources to slow the growing burden.
plos-pone-0344138:
Bowen and colleagues, in a 2026 study, collect herpes simplex virus samples from a remote pastoralist population in northern Namibia. The virus infects more than half of all adults worldwide and can cause anything from no symptoms to rare, deadly brain infection. Yet nearly all virus genomes on record come from Europe and North America, leaving Africa badly under-sampled.

Working in desert settlements far from labs, the team used treated cards that keep DNA stable on mouth and genital swabs, so samples could travel safely. The virus genomes they recovered, the first ever reported from Namibia, fit within the range of variation already known from other African strains. No strange new branch appeared, but the gap in the map is smaller now. The authors offer their field method as a model for studying viruses in other remote and under-served places, where disease burdens are often guessed rather than measured.
plos-pone-0345338:
Tianyu Wang and colleagues tested whether shrinking liver fat over just two weeks improves blood vessel health. Fatty liver disease tied to metabolism raises heart and vessel risk, but quick benefits were unproven. Their 2026 trial assigned adults with the disease, or at risk of it, to a very low-carbohydrate or a low-calorie diet.

Liver fat fell clearly in the whole group, with no real difference between the two diets. A stiffness measure for arteries improved, a standard heart-risk score dropped, and vessel widening response grew slightly. Liver fat loss also tracked with a lower resting heart rate. Wang and colleagues read the pattern as early vessel gains arriving alongside liver fat loss.
plos-pone-0345938:
Aqian Yu and Jingjing An score the quality of stroke care worldwide in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper, drawing on the 2021 round of the Global Burden of Disease project. They built a quality of care index for stroke and its three subtypes, covering bleeding and blocked-vessel forms, and a ratio comparing women's scores with men's.

Stroke rates fell from 1990 to 2021 while care quality rose, and the gender gap narrowed toward equality for most subtypes. Richer, more developed settings scored higher on quality but sometimes showed wider gender gaps. Wide differences between countries, sexes, and age groups remain, and the authors argue those gaps should guide where health systems improve first.
plos-pone-0346738:
Sainan Li and Jing Wu present a new signal processing method for pulling repeating pulse patterns out of messy recordings. Many machines and bodies produce such rhythms, from vibrating engines to heartbeats and brain waves, but noise and overlap make them hard to isolate. Their 2026 paper builds the method on a mathematical tool called the Blaschke Transform.

The algorithm first marks which frequency bands matter, then splits the signal into separate rhythm modes using a bank of filters. A final step merges modes that repeat at similar rates, preventing the signal from being chopped into too many pieces. Tests on simulated data, machine vibration, and brain and heart recordings showed clean separation and noise removal.
plos-pone-0346838:
Vasyl Kulish, Sergiy Boruk, and Igor Winkler published this 2026 study of clearing a particular microplastic from water. Tiny styrene-based plastic particles resist settling on their own. In jar tests with an alum-based commercial coagulant, the team watched particles clump into flocs and sink, then tracked how the settled layer compacted over two days.

A small dose of coagulant shrank the sediment layer and made it denser, firmer, and harder to stir back up, with most settling done within a day. The authors pinpoint a best dose range for treating contaminated water.
plos-pone-0347038:
James D. Thomson and David F. Andrews report a rare thirty-three-year watch on glacier lilies growing in a protected transplant garden. Each year the buried bulbs were dug up, photographed, and weighed, building a life record few plant studies can match. Their 2026 paper asks what making fruit costs a long-lived plant and how such plants manage their size and aging.

Plants took five or six years to reach flowering size. Making a single fruit cost a plant roughly a twelfth of the weight it would otherwise have gained. Plants held their size by splitting now and then. Deaths were rare; a few faded slowly in a pattern like aging, while others died suddenly from fungus. More years, the authors say, will settle how these lilies age.
plos-pone-0347538:
Per Morten Fredriksen and co-workers compare two simple body measures in children: the familiar body mass index and the ratio of waist size to height. Which one flags heart and fitness risks better is still argued. Their 2026 study uses yearly checks on close to twenty-three hundred Norwegian children aged six to twelve, gathered through a school health project.

Both measures pointed the same way: higher values went with more body fat, higher blood pressure, worse blood fats, and lower fitness. The waist ratio edged ahead slightly for blood fats and fitness outcomes. The authors suggest using the two together in screening, since waist size adds a window on belly fat that the index alone can miss.
plos-pone-0347638:
Fawn Harrad-Hyde, Christina Faull, and Linda Birt follow the hidden work of family carers in this 2026 study. Their relatives live in care homes in England with cognitive impairment. Moving into a home does not end family care. Twenty-nine carers described what they still do, from the move itself through later stages of decline. The authors sort that labour into six kinds of work.

Body work covers hands-on physical help. Comfort work soothes and reassures. Information work and coordination work keep staff, services, and family aligned. Safety work watches for risks in an unfamiliar setting. Biography work keeps the person's story and identity alive for those caring for them. Every form persisted across the whole care journey, changing shape rather than disappearing. Carers said the point was dignity: protecting health, wellbeing, and the abilities their relative still had.
plos-pone-0347738:
Abdulrahman Sharif, Maha Hamood, and Kirtiwant Ghadle present a math study of a loaded equation system. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The model mixes a fractional derivative, which gives equations a memory of past states. It adds sudden impulses and hidden nonlinear terms. Its edge conditions use integrals, not fixed values.

Two classic fixed-point theorems prove that solutions exist. Under tighter rules, the solution is the only one. The team also shows the solutions stay stable under small shocks. Computer runs with a standard scheme back the theory. Systems with memory and shocks model real things. Drug dosing and circuit breaks are two such cases. The proofs widen where these models can be trusted.
plos-pone-0347838:
Bobo Li designs a smarter controller for a hydraulic lifting arm's wrist. His engineering paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Old controllers lag and track paths loosely. That matters when a machine arm must place loads with care. His design builds the arm's physics straight into the control loop. Smart algorithms then fine-tune the loop as it runs.

Tests showed tight path control. The worst tracking error was a fraction of a millimeter. Fault spotting scored very high. Energy use stayed lean as well. The design beat several recent rivals on accuracy, steadiness, and speed. It targets smart factories, where lifting robots must be strong and exact.
plos-pone-0348138:
Xingxing Zhang and Han Liu measure turbulence in a jet of fluid that runs along a wall inside a closed box and then meets an end wall. Such flows appear in ventilation, cooling, and many machines, but their rough, swirling behavior near the end wall is poorly charted. Their 2026 study films tracer particles to map motion across zones downstream.

Turbulence patterns changed character zone by zone as the jet neared the end wall. One middle zone behaved like a fully spread radial flow. Farther on, maps from different viewing planes stopped matching, and peak swirling rose with flow speed in one plane only. Small changes in water depth mattered little for intensity but did move stress peaks. Engineers gain a finer map for predicting confined jets.
plos-pone-0348438:
Sanja Balalic and co-workers ask nursing home staff what good they expect social robots might do in daily elder care. Staff shortages strain care for older adults living in institutions. Their 2026 study holds two rounds of group talks with twenty-four care workers across three nursing homes, first gathering ideas and then testing them across groups.

Staff hoped robots could cut workload and mental strain while lifting the mood at work. For residents, reminders could support self-care, and robot company could ease lonely hours. Time saved might free workers to focus on residents who need help but rarely ask. Worries included gaps in technical skill and families who might resist. The expectations map where trials of care robots should start.
plos-pone-0349238:
Maia R Supple and Jaemin Lee studied how insects feed on leaves in lowland rainforest on Moorea, a remote island in French Polynesia. Plant invaders are blamed for insect losses worldwide, yet island food webs are less well known. The team scored bite and damage marks on fallen leaves from twelve tree and plant kinds: native, brought in but calm, and invasive.

Invasive plants carried far fewer kinds of feeding damage and far less feeding overall. In web maps they sat at the edges with weak links, while native and calm introduced plants sat at the centre. Calm introduced plants matched natives closely, which hints that insect feeding may help keep some newcomers in check.
plos-pone-0349338:
Fengjun Zhang and colleagues combined gene datasets and machine learning to find blood-or-tissue markers that could diagnose chronic obstructive pulmonary disease earlier. The lung disease creeps up slowly and is often caught late. Two public datasets were merged to find genes behaving differently in patients, and a combined machine learning model screened them down to candidates.

Two genes, ITGB2 and HNRNPAB, emerged as the strongest diagnostic signals. The team probed the pathways around them, the immune cell mix in patient samples, and genetic evidence for cause, then confirmed the markers with laboratory tests on real samples. Early, accurate diagnosis changes COPD care, so a validated two-gene signal is a concrete step toward a practical test.
plos-pone-0349438:
Bin Tang and co-authors asked whether using computers and other information tools actually helps rural schoolchildren learn and grow. They studied third and fourth graders in poor areas of western China, using survey data collected in two rounds across 2019 and 2020. Their 2026 analysis matched similar students with and without heavy technology use, then compared how each group changed over time.

Technology use showed no clear gain in test-based thinking skills, though the trend leaned slightly positive. Frequent use did seem to make children more open and fonder of school and teachers, yet it was also tied to more self-blame and worry. Effects were stronger for older children and for poorer families. The authors urge support that keeps the benefits while limiting the harms.
plos-pone-0349838:
Bo Sook Han and co-authors asked whether eye-socket scans can show how active thyroid eye disease is. The disease swells eye muscles and fat, and judging its inflammatory activity guides treatment timing. Their 2026 study measured muscle, fat, and tear gland volumes and densities in eighty-five patients and fifteen controls.

Eye muscle volume ran significantly larger in active disease than in inactive disease or controls. Fat density, a sign of inflamed waterlogged tissue, also ran higher in active cases. A thyroid-stimulating antibody level separated the groups as well. Fat volume and muscle density did not separate them. Han and colleagues propose scan measures as objective support for activity grading.
plos-pone-0350638:
Xinyao Zhu and colleagues combined several computer methods in 2026 to study how phenolic pollutants in water might promote prostate cancer. These hormone mimicking chemicals are widespread, and one fat making gene drew their attention.

The team predicted pollutant targets, crossed them with cancer genes, and used machine learning to refine a core set. Checks against tumor data and single cell records showed where the key gene acts. Docking simulations tested how firmly the chemicals bind their targets. The layered analysis builds a plausible chain from water pollution to tumor growth, while remaining a computer based case needing lab proof.
plos-pone-0350738:
Yosia Mugume and co-authors reported a gene find in the model plant Arabidopsis in 2026. Plants that overproduce a fat cutting enzyme grow stunted because they flood themselves with a defence hormone. A screen for mutants that recover normal growth pointed to a second gene.

The rescuing change sits in a lipoxygenase gene needed to build the defence hormone jasmonic acid. A single letter change near the enzyme's iron site likely blocks it from processing its raw material. Mutant plants made far less hormone and grew closer to normal. The result maps one clear step in the chain from leaf fat to defence signalling.
plos-pone-0350838:
İrfan Kiliç and co-authors turned gearbox vibration readings into pictures so an image network could hunt for gear faults. Sensors on a test gearbox produced streams of numbers, hard for vision models to read raw. The team summarized each signal by its highest, lowest, and average values and painted those into the red, green, and blue channels of synthetic images, then trained a segmentation network on them.

After only ten training rounds, the model classified faults with accuracy above ninety-nine percent on the benchmark set. Painting numbers as colors let a vision architecture do what it does best, finding patterns in space. Factory engineers chase exactly this: worn gears caught from vibration before they seize. Whether the trick survives noisier real plants is the open test, but the representation itself is the contribution.
plos-pone-0350938:
Hasina Al Harthi and co-authors built a fair scoring tool for grant choices in Oman. Peer review of grant bids can be hit-or-miss and prone to bias. Their 2026 study mixed a scan of past work, a survey at a Muscat hospital, expert rounds, and a method that weighs each rule by paired comparisons.

Ten rules for judging bids came out of the work. Worth, ethics, newness, and fit with big goals sat with ease of doing, impact, cost sense, and team strength. Experts set the weight of each rule by judging them two at a time. Al Harthi and colleagues offer the scorecard as a clear, open way for panels to judge bids the same way each time.
plos-pone-0351138:
Brain implants reached through blood vessels avoid open surgery, but today's versions trail wires through the body to a chest unit. Yi-De Tai and colleagues tested whether power could instead be beamed wirelessly to such an implant, in this 2026 PLOS One engineering study.

They designed sending and receiving coils sized for vessel and skull limits, then checked them in computer models, on benches, and in living tissue. The tests measured how much power crosses, how well coils tolerate misalignment, and whether tissue heating stays within safety limits. Removing the wires would cut infection and clotting risks, so the results mark a step toward a fully implanted device.
plos-pone-0351338:
Electrodes on the skin can reveal how muscles fire after spinal cord injury, yet therapists rarely use the data in clinics. Nadeen Al Awamry and colleagues interviewed ten physical and occupational therapists about that gap, in this 2026 PLOS One qualitative study.

Therapists saw real value in the readings: hard numbers to confirm progress after incomplete injuries and to set shared goals with patients. Barriers included time, training, equipment cost, and trouble turning traces into treatment decisions. Supportive clinics and simpler tools were named as helpers. The authors say adoption depends less on the technology than on fitting it into daily rehabilitation work.
plos-pone-0351438:
Sabiha Khatoon and Mohammed A Junaid tested whether folic acid, a B vitamin best known for protecting unborn babies, can boost a missing enzyme in Fabry disease. In Fabry disease a faulty gene lowers an enzyme that clears fatty waste, so waste builds up in organs. Lab work used human cells in dishes and a pure form of the enzyme.

Folic acid raised both enzyme amounts and enzyme activity in a dose linked way, in cells from men and women alike. It also protected the enzyme from a blocking drug and deepened that drugs repair effect in cells from a patient. Even small lifts in enzyme activity may help patients, so a cheap vitamin lead is worth careful follow up.
plos-pone-0351538:
Saleh Al Omar and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One study of whether a structured research course changes nursing students' attitudes toward research. Sixty-two Saudi undergraduates completed a validated attitude questionnaire before and after a fourteen-week course at a public university. The course covered research skills and how findings are used in clinical practice.

Overall attitudes improved significantly after the course, with the clearest gains in confidence about research skills and in valuing research at the bedside. Personal interest in research and belief in its usefulness, however, did not budge. Male students with lower grades showed the largest shifts. The authors advise teachers to use more varied methods if they also want students to find research genuinely interesting.
plos-pone-0351738:
When an opioid overdose stops the heart, ambulance crews already carry naloxone, a drug that reverses opioid effects within minutes. Hania Siddiqui and colleagues reviewed whether giving it during such cardiac arrests helps patients, in this 2026 PLOS One systematic review.

The team searched three medical databases through late 2024 and found only eight studies that fit their rules, too different from each other to combine into one pooled number. Reviewers screened papers in pairs and checked each study for bias. The small, mixed evidence base is itself the main message: crews still lack a clear answer on whether naloxone changes survival or recovery here.
plos-pone-0351838:
Ben Langford and colleagues found a snag in a promising way to spot lung disease in calves from their breath. Diseased breath carries telltale gases, but farm calves often receive antibiotics, and drugs may rewrite that chemical signature. The team analyzed breath from sixty-five calves and then dosed healthy calves with a common antibiotic to isolate the drug's own effect.

Some gases did rise at disease onset, yet the clearest split between sick and healthy calves came after antibiotics were given. In healthy calves, the drug alone shifted breath gases within an hour, with more changes inside a day. So a breath test may partly be reading the medicine, not the illness. Any farm test built on breath will need to account for treatment, or risk calling treated calves sick for the wrong reason.
plos-pone-0351938:
Angela Claire Thornton and seven co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One interview study on chronic pain at work. Employers and managers had trialed a digital toolkit that helps workers manage pain on the job. Fifteen stakeholders from twelve firms discussed how the toolkit might work in real workplaces. Their accounts were grouped into themes.

Three themes stood out. First, chronic pain is an invisible disability that firms underestimate. Second, line managers differ widely in how well they support affected staff. Third, control over adjustments is contested between employer and worker. Stakeholders wanted the toolkit. They wanted manager training just as much. The authors say better-equipped managers could cut sickness absence. They could also ease the strain of working while unwell.
plos-pone-0352138:
Chen and colleagues, in a 2026 study, settle an argument about concrete made with steel slag, a waste product of steelmaking, in place of crushed stone. Builders like the idea of recycling slag, but whether the swap makes concrete stronger, and which swap works best, was disputed. The team cast four versions and broke them in the lab.

The four mixes used plain stone, coarse slag with natural sand, stone with fine slag, and slag for both coarse and fine parts. In squeezing, bending, and splitting tests, every slag version beat plain concrete, and the all-slag mix was strongest. Fine slag helped more than coarse slag, and microscope and X-ray checks showed why the inner structure differed. The authors caution that their conditions were specific, yet under them, grinding slag fine and using it widely looks like the best recipe for stronger concrete from waste.
plos-pone-0352238:
Yuxuan Qian and six colleagues report a 2026 plant study on a rice gene moved into lettuce. The gene helps rice absorb nitrate, a key form of nitrogen fertiliser. Lettuce often wastes nitrogen, so the team tested whether the gene helps when nitrogen is scarce. Four high-expressing lettuce lines were grown under normal and low nitrogen.

The engineered lettuce held more chlorophyll and more glutathione, a protective molecule. Its defence enzymes against oxidative damage also worked harder. Inside the leaves, nitrate, ammonium, amino acids, and soluble protein all rose. Enzymes that process nitrogen became more active too. Plant size barely changed, though. The gene mainly improved internal chemistry and nitrogen use, which could help growers cut fertiliser without losing crop quality.
plos-pone-0352438:
Gao and colleagues tested when to move young maize plants into fields in a 2026 study. Growers sometimes raise seedlings first and plant them out to fill gaps, but moving plants can stress them and cut the harvest. Field trials at two sites compared direct seeding with planting out at three young leaf stages.

Moved plants grew smaller roots and leaves than direct-seeded plants and lost yield in the end. Stress showed up in lower leaf efficiency, even though the plants used water more tightly. Moving plants at the middle stage, with three leaves and one heart leaf, came closest to direct seeding. That timing offers the least loss when replanting cannot be avoided.
plos-pone-0352638:
Chen and colleagues studied how to protect glazed parts of ancient Chinese buildings in a 2026 paper. Glazed tiles crown roofs and walls but crack and powder after long exposure to heat, damp, and acid air. The team documented decay forms and reproduced damage processes in the lab.

Two strengthening liquids were tested on weakened tile bodies, applied with an alcohol solvent. The goal is a treatment that firms the tile without changing its look. Heritage repairs fail when coatings peel or gloss clashes with old glaze. Careful material matching, shown here, helps restorers keep historic roofs both sound and authentic.
plos-pone-0352938:
Zarmeen Nasim and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One analysis of dengue fever in Pakistan from 2012 to 2022. They used lab-confirmed cases. They adjusted the counts for how likely people are to seek care and be tested. The team estimated rates by province, district, age, and sex. The aim was to fill gaps left by under-reporting and uneven diagnosis.

Dengue rates climbed over the decade in every age group. Working-age adults carried the highest rates. Men were hit more than women throughout. Sindh province stood out with by far the highest rates in 2022. Baluchistan had the lowest. The authors say the widening, uneven burden demands stronger mosquito control. It also demands better case counting, since official figures miss much of the disease.
plos-pone-0353738:
Christina Due Svendsen and four colleagues test a microbial hunch. Do the microbes in the mouth and lungs differ in people with heart disease? Their study came from Norway. It appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The group had one hundred and twenty-seven patients with chronic lung disease. It also had one hundred and one healthy controls. All had heart scans to grade artery calcium and narrowing. All gave mouth rinses and lung washings for DNA sequencing.

Microbe communities did differ between lung patients and controls. The gap showed in the mouth samples. But people with and without coronary disease looked alike. No meaningful differences appeared in either site. The negative result argues against a simple airway signature of heart disease. At least, none that current methods can find.
plos-pone-0353838:
Lan Zhang led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study linking body-clock disruption to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a long-term lung illness. They merged several public lung data sets, screened clock-related genes that change in the disease, and let machine learning pick the strongest candidates. They then checked the winner in another cohort and in single cells.

One gene, CHRNA1, rose consistently and tracked with inflammatory immune cells, mostly in the lung's B cells. Zhang built a risk model around such signals, while noting the clock-targeting idea still needs testing in patients before clinical use.
plos-pone-0353938:
Mahoukpégo Luc Zinzinhédo and co-authors stress-test crop yield prediction models by feeding them thousands of deliberately flawed datasets. Real farm data arrive with gaps and tangled measures, and advice on cleaning them is scattered. The simulation varied dataset size, predictor count, missing values, and overlap among predictors, crossed with cleaning choices, across seven learning methods, then repeated the checks on five real crop datasets.

Missing data hurt accuracy badly, tangled predictors faked one kind of score while worsening another, and bigger datasets reliably helped. Filling gaps by regression worked best overall, and one forest method stayed steadiest across conditions. Zinzinhédo and colleagues warn that no cleaning recipe wins everywhere, so modelers must match preparation to the dataset in hand.
plos-pone-0354038:
Alina Maryum and seven colleagues build a cheap machine-learning screen for osteoporosis, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study aimed at clinics with few resources. The standard bone scan is costly and often unavailable where patients are poorest. Instead, their model uses records from two Pakistani hospitals and leans on simple inputs: blood group, blood calcium and potassium, weight, and vitamin D levels.

An ensemble of classifiers sorted patients by osteoporosis severity with accuracy around nine in ten. A second model estimated spine bone density moderately well from age, weight, blood group, and vitamin D. If confirmed in larger samples, screening from routine blood tests could flag at-risk patients long before a fracture.
plos-pone-0354138:
Shupeng Wu and three colleagues published this 2026 computer study of bisphenol A, a common plastics chemical, and myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune disease that weakens muscles. Genes tied to the chemical and to the disease were gathered from public databases, overlapped, and screened with machine learning, then checked with molecular simulations and experiments.

Three genes emerged as plausible links, touching ion transport, nerve-muscle signaling, and immune activation. Wu stresses the evidence shows links, not causes, built mostly in computers, but it sketches how an everyday chemical might nudge a rare disease process.
plos-pone-0354238:
Clément Gouraud and co-authors ask in 2026 whether long COVID patients who also receive a functional somatic disorder diagnosis report worse quality of life. Data came from a specialist programme for people with lasting symptoms after COVID, using a standard health survey that gives physical and mental scores. Most patients in the sample carried the extra diagnosis.

Quality of life was clearly impaired overall, yet scores did not differ by the extra diagnosis once other factors were counted. Lower scores linked instead to depression, anxiety, pain, and low activity, with physical scores also tied to sex, hospital stay, and symptom length. Care should target those drivers, the authors suggest.
plos-pone-0354338: Natural wastewater treatment — multi-stage systems — can harbor viable opportunistic pathogens. This paper documented their persistence. The findings warn that ‘natural’ treatment isn’t automatically safe — with implications for water reuse.
plos-pone-0354738:
Massae and colleagues, writing in 2026, ask why vacuum-assisted birth is so seldom used at a large hospital in Tanzania. A vacuum device can help deliver a baby when the last stage of labor stalls, the mother is worn out, or the baby is in distress. When it is not used, more births end in surgery that might have been avoided.

The team spoke in depth with twelve clinicians who had experience with the method. Two kinds of blocks came up. At the hospital level, gear was scarce, some devices worked poorly, and team choices were not well coordinated. At the personal level, clinicians feared bad outcomes and felt short on skill and hands-on practice. The authors argue that working gear, better training, and stronger team routines could raise use and cut needless surgical births.
plos-pone-0355238:
Parveen Kumari and a large team compared three ways of teaching a computer to hear emotion in speech. Each way was tested under two rules. Under the easy rule, the same actors appear in training and testing. Under the honest rule, test voices are strangers. Their 2026 study used a standard acted emotion corpus. It combined handcrafted sound features with deep network embeddings in a lightweight hybrid.

The hybrid won under both rules. Every method lost ground when voices changed, exposing how inflated easy-split scores are. The team's real contribution is discipline. It used identical preprocessing, repeated runs, and class-by-class error audits. A small web tool lets readers try the model live. Speech emotion systems headed for call centers and tutoring need exactly this kind of honest benchmarking.
plos-pone-0355338: Measuring body composition in anesthetized dogs — via multifrequency bioimpedance — depends on electrode choice. This paper compared clip and needle electrodes. The comparison guides veterinary anesthesiologists toward measurements they can trust during surgery.
plos-pone-0355738:
Gabriel Bertochi and co-authors test in 2026 whether heavy or explosive warm up moves boost a standing jump a few minutes later, and whether men and women differ. Trained adults tried six preparation moves across separate visits, including squats and drop jumps, some with a weighted vest. Jump height was measured before and four minutes after each move.

No preparation clearly raised jump height in that window, for the whole group or for either sex alone. The authors suggest the boost may be tiny after a full warm up already done, and coaches should weigh personal traits rather than expect a set gain. Sex showed no effect on the result.
plos-pone-0355838:
Piyanut Ratphibun Yamashita and co-authors built personal computer models to judge breast cancer risk from gene activity plus cell signalling. Standard risk tools ignore molecular detail, which limits personal prevention advice. Their 2026 framework merged each woman's gene profile with a dynamic simulation of signalling pathways for thirty subjects.

Features drawn from the simulations split the women into four risk clusters with clearly different cancer-free spans. The highest-risk group stayed cancer-free for the shortest time, by a wide margin. Its signature was overactive growth signalling through a well-known pathway chain. Yamashita and colleagues say pathway behaviour adds information beyond static gene readings, and could guide tailored prevention if larger studies confirm it.
plos-pone-0355938:
Hilde EM Augusteijn and three colleagues tested what shapes peer review judgments in psychology, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Reviewers judge manuscripts for quality, but surface features may sway them apart from the science itself. The team studied how a manuscript's own traits shape the quality scores reviewers give scientific work in the field.

Augusteijn's findings expose which features, such as writing flair, formatting, or framing, move judgments. That matters for fairness: if polish beats substance, good work in plain dress gets rejected while weak work in fine dress passes. Journals can respond with reviewer guidance or structured forms. Psychology is a fitting test bed, since it has led debates about research quality and reform in recent years.
plos-pone-0356138:
Ahmad Basil Nasir and colleagues mined American electronic health records for more than one and a half million adults with type 2 diabetes. They asked whether the diabetes drug a person takes tracks with later cognitive decline. Their 2026 retrospective study matched patients across five regimens, with metformin alone as the yardstick. It followed diagnoses of mild cognitive disorder, Alzheimer's disease, and vascular dementia over up to fourteen years.

Adding a GLP-1 drug to metformin was linked to roughly half the risk of vascular dementia and Alzheimer's. It was also linked to a lower rate of mild impairment. Adding an SGLT-2 drug cut vascular dementia only. Insulin alone looked worst on every outcome, likely reflecting more severe disease. The authors stress records show association, not proof.
plos-pone-0356238:
Xiangjun Li, Ruitao Li, Zhui Tu, and Qingting Wei built FusionPHI, a model that predicts which bacteria a given virus can infect. Phage therapy needs that information before it can match a bacteria-killing virus to a patient's strain. Their 2026 paper feeds the model three views of each partner. They are genome letter statistics, protein chemistry, and evolved gene motif embeddings. A two-stage attention mechanism fuses them.

The model scored strongly on its test data. Ablation tests showed each information stream earns its place, and so does the attention fusion. A case check on a textbook E. coli phage behaved as hoped. Faster, trustworthy matching could make phage therapy practical against antibiotic-resistant infections, instead of a laboratory fishing expedition.
plos-pone-0356638:
Lu Dai and coauthors published a 2026 gene study in PLOS ONE on acute liver failure triggered by hepatitis B, hunting for biomarkers where two forces meet: oxidative stress and immune infiltration. Both damage the failing liver, but their combined signature had never been mined. The team sifted a public gene dataset for genes that differed in disease, belonged to oxidative stress lists, and sat in key co-expression modules. Two machine learning methods then voted the list down.

Five candidate genes survived, and checking them in a second dataset trimmed the panel to four: CLU, APOH, AMBP, and GPX8. Each gene alone carried useful diagnostic signal, and enrichment analysis tied all four to metabolic processes. A microRNA network around them was mapped, and candidate drugs predicted. They present the four-gene signature as a starting point for a blood test and for mechanistic work, not yet a clinical tool.
plos-pone-0356838:
Niroshan Chandrajith Lokunarangoda and colleagues publish a plan in 2026 for a systematic review of dengue's long-term effects on the heart. Dengue, a mosquito-borne disease common in tropical regions, is usually seen as a short illness that patients recover from fully. Reports of heart problems weeks or months later, though, have raised doubts about that picture.

Under the registered protocol, the team will gather human studies that report heart or blood-vessel outcomes at least four weeks after dengue infection. They will search seven databases, screen studies in pairs, and weigh the quality of the evidence before combining results. Outcomes range from strokes and rhythm problems to subtle changes picked up on scans and blood tests. The finished review should show whether survivors need heart follow-up and where the evidence is still too thin to judge.
plos-pone-0357038:

Blocked leg arteries limit walking, and a questionnaire score can capture what patients can actually do. The team scored patients before the procedure and six months later, grouping them as stayed low, stayed higher, or climbed from low to higher, then tracked heart and limb events.

Patients stuck at low capacity faced the highest later risks, including a markedly higher death risk than those who stayed higher. Encouragingly, patients who climbed into the higher group ended with risk much like those who had always been higher. Heffron and colleagues say helping patients gain real activity after the procedure may matter as much as the procedure itself.
plos-pone-0357938:

The exposure is vanadium citrate, a compound of the metal vanadium, given to the animals.

The effects reported depend on both sex and dose, varying between male and female rats and with how much compound they received. Sex- and dose-dependent results warn against treating one group's response as universal. Toxicologists and researchers studying vanadium, which is also marketed in supplements, are the readers for tissue-level evidence like this.
plos-pone-0358038:

Yadav's group showed that Tceal7 is switched on through calcineurin signaling, under control of a protein called BRG1, and that it promotes myoblast development. Each defined link like this adds a piece to the puzzle of muscle building. That puzzle matters for diseases that waste muscle and for injuries that heal poorly. Knowing the chain also gives researchers points where they might one day intervene to help muscle grow.
plos-pone-0358338:

Coaches often guide movement with a hand on a shoulder or back, but comfort may depend on who touches, where, and how well the two know each other. They asked female university students in Japan to rate dozens of imagined scenarios, varying the toucher's gender, the body region, and whether the toucher was a teacher, close friend, or acquaintance.

Across both sets of scenarios, contact from men caused more discomfort than contact from women, and some body regions were consistently more sensitive than others. For teachers, the toucher's gender and the body region mattered on their own, with no extra combined effect. Among friends and acquaintances, closeness changed how strongly gender mattered. The findings give physical education programs concrete factors to weigh in guidance on instructional touch.
plos-pone-0358538:

Zhou's system learns from those human-object interactions to judge which clips look normal and which do not. Unusual handling of an object can flag an event that a watcher should review. Using weak labels cuts training cost a great deal. The method suits security and safety settings where staff cannot label hours of video by hand but still need alerts they can trust.
plos-pone-0358738:

Twenty-six fatty acids were identified. In dishes, the extracts slowed two bacterial species modestly and fungi not at all. The dataset is a foundation for anyone mining fly larvae for drug leads.
plos-pone-0358938: Biello and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a long-term study in New England called RISE-NE. plos-pone-0359538: Bozděch, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on junior girls' tennis over two decades. The study tracks rankings on the ITF World Tennis Tour Juniors from 2004 to 2025. plos-pone-0359638:
