pmc-13648938: 2026 research into Repeated Thrombolysis Using Tenecteplase in a Pa delivered answers. The data was compelling. Those who study will use it in their work. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
pmc-13649438: A 2026 contribution, Traditional Chinese and Western medicine-integra, pushed the boundary, the novel approach. The paper lasts as a quiet witness to its time. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
pmc-13650538: Fluorinated pore walls boost PFAS capture in : a 2026 study that broke new ground. The conclusions matter. The scholarly record preserves it. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
pmc-13652538: Scientists examined The structural context of mutations in proteins in 2026, the biomedical insights. Time has kept the file intact through the years. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
pmc-3069738:
Winn, Ballard, Cowtan, and co-authors give an overview of the CCP4 suite and its current developments. CCP4 is a long-running collection of programs for macromolecular crystallography, the method that reveals protein shapes from crystal diffraction. The suite joins tools for each stage, from raw data to finished structure.

Their overview describes what the suite contains and where development was heading in 2011. A shared, maintained suite keeps methods consistent across hundreds of labs. It also lowers the barrier for new groups, who gain a tested pipeline instead of assembling software alone.
pmc-6086938:
Yury Goltsev, Nikolay Samusik, Julia Kennedy-Darling, and coauthors profiled mouse spleen tissue with CODEX imaging in 2018. CODEX tags antibodies with DNA barcodes and reads them out in repeated rounds. One tissue slice can thus show dozens of proteins at once.

The team built detailed maps of healthy spleens and of spleens from a lupus mouse model. The maps reveal how immune cells arrange into neighborhoods and how disease reshapes them. Seeing arrangement, not just cell counts, exposes contacts that drive immune behavior. The method points toward richer tissue maps in human disease studies.
pmc-6351938:
Emanuele Rinninella, Pauline Raoul, Marco Cintoni, and coauthors asked what a healthy gut microbiota looks like in 2019. Each person carries a unique gut community that aids digestion, guards the gut wall, and trains immunity. Its makeup shifts with age, place, and diet.

The review describes the main bacterial groups in a healthy gut and what they do. It then shows how antibiotics, birth mode, and illness disturb that balance. No single perfect profile exists, which the authors stress. The paper gives clinicians a grounded picture of normal before judging what counts as disturbed.
pmc-7088738:
Xin Zou, Ke Chen, Jiawei Zou, and coauthors analyzed ACE2 expression at single-cell level early in the COVID-19 outbreak in 2020. The new virus enters cells through the ACE2 receptor, as the earlier SARS virus did. Lung cells carrying ACE2 were thought to be its main targets.

Scanning public single-cell data, the team found ACE2 in a small set of lung cells that also make mucus-related proteins. They flag higher expression patterns that might mark greater risk. The quick analysis, done from open data, helped focus early thinking on which tissues the virus could reach.
pmc-7250738:
Jing Yang and many co-authors set out shared guidelines in 2020 for research on epithelial-mesenchymal transition, a process often shortened to EMT. During this process, cells that normally sit in ordered sheets loosen their grip, change shape, and gain the ability to move and invade nearby tissue. It shows up in normal development, in wound healing, and in diseases such as cancer and scarring disorders.

The problem the guidelines tackle is disagreement, since labs were using the same terms for different cell states and drawing clashing conclusions. The authors lay out agreed definitions and describe which traits should be measured before a change counts as this transition. For a fast moving field, a shared language lets results from different labs be compared with confidence.
pmc-7486838:
John Donnelly and colleagues issued in 2019 a revised set of shared definitions for invasive fungal disease. Two research groups stand behind the update, one European and one international consortium devoted to fungal disease study. Earlier versions of these definitions had become a common language that let hospitals and researchers describe the same illnesses in the same way.

The revision spells out what counts as proven, probable, or possible infection, and which lab tests and scans support each level. It also folds in newer diagnostic tools that had appeared since the previous edition. Clear case definitions sound dry, but trials of new antifungal drugs and comparisons between hospitals stand or fall on exactly this kind of agreement.
pmc-7755038:
Gregory Roth and a global team of collaborators charted in 2020 the worldwide burden of cardiovascular diseases and their risk factors across three decades. Heart and blood vessel diseases, above all ischemic heart disease and stroke, are the leading cause of death on the planet. They also account for a large share of the years people live with disability.

The study reviews the total burden from 1990 to 2019, covering more than a dozen underlying causes of cardiovascular death and a set of major risk factors. It shows where the burden is rising, where it is falling, and which risks drive it in each region. Health systems use this accounting to decide where screening and prevention will save the most lives.
pmc-8446938:
The NCD Risk Factor Collaboration pooled data in 2021 on high blood pressure, covering two hundred countries and three decades. Hypertension is easy to detect in primary care, and cheap treatments control it well, yet control remains poor in much of the world. The analysis combined more than twelve hundred representative studies with well over one hundred million participants.

The authors measure how common hypertension was from 1990 to 2019, and how far each country got with detecting it, treating it, and bringing it under control. The results expose a stark divide, with some health systems controlling most cases and others very few. The study is a scorecard for one of the most fixable major health risks.
pmc-8728138:
David Wishart and colleagues presented HMDB 5.0 in 2021, the 2022 edition of the Human Metabolome Database. The database has provided reference information on human metabolites, the small molecules produced by the body, since 2007. It records their biological roles, the diseases they connect to, and their chemical properties.

The authors describe how the resource grew and changed over fifteen years, with far more metabolites and richer detail on each. They also explain the tools for searching and comparing entries. Doctors and researchers use the HMDB when a blood or tissue measurement turns up an unfamiliar molecule, making it a standard desk reference for the study of metabolism.
podcast-tuckercarlson-mXO-EvCtY38:
Quarterback Aaron Rodgers joins Tucker Carlson's podcast for a long, unfiltered talk. Rodgers, one of the NFL's great passers, became a public lightning rod over his vaccine stance. With Carlson he ranges far past football, into the stories that made him a culture-war figure.

He talks about Jeffrey Epstein's death, his psychedelic experiences, and fake vaccine cards in the NFL. He also discusses Pat Tillman, who left football for the Army and was killed in Afghanistan. Carlson lets him run on each. The segment is a star athlete off the leash, kept as a record of views his league would rather he kept quiet.
poe-narrative-arthur-gordon-pym-1838:
Edgar Allan Poe wrote his sole long tale, the Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym, in 1838. Pym stows away on a brig bound for the south seas. Mutiny, wreck, and thirst drive the crew to the edge of death. Poe tells the tale as a true log found in print.

A rescue ship turns out to be a death ship full of corpses. Pym sails on south past ice to a warm sea and a black isle. White birds, strange signs, and a vast white form close the tale in mist. The book is the root text of the polar tale of dread.
solenopedie-ou-revelation-d-un-nouveau-s: Solénopédie, 1838. The phrenological education. This book preserves that work. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. History keeps its place secure. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it.
the-principles-of-phrenology-1838: The Principles of Phrenology, 1838. The phrenological principles. This book preserves that work. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. History keeps its place secure. Scholars will consult it. The text survives intact.
tob-0038:
Senator Frank Church led the Senate committee that pried open the secrets of United States intelligence in 1975. Its interim report on alleged assassination plots examined claims that the CIA had plotted to kill foreign leaders, among them Fidel Castro of Cuba and Patrice Lumumba of the Congo.

Rafael Trujillo and Ngo Dinh Diem also figure in the charges and evidence. The committee traced orders, memos, and denials through layers of official fog. Its findings shocked the country and led in time to a standing ban on political assassination by United States agents. Modern oversight of the spy agencies starts here.
tob-0138:
A second catalog copy of John Robison's 1797 Proofs of a Conspiracy presents the famous exposé of an alleged Illuminati plot. Secret societies and Masonic lodges, in Robison's telling, concealed a hidden hand behind the French Revolution and a campaign against all religions and governments of Europe. The duplicate record mirrors the book's own wide, repeated circulation.

Robison's charges taught the English-speaking world to fear the secret society as a political weapon. Presidents and pamphleteers answered him, and the template he set, suppressed order, infiltrated lodges, revolution as engineered plot, still structures conspiracy writing. Readers can consult either copy; the text is the founding document in duplicate.
tob-13138:
E. A. Wallis Budge, the great Victorian Egyptologist, gave English readers the Egyptian Book of the Dead in his pioneering translation. Spells, hymns, and underworld maps were buried with pharaohs and scribes to secure safe passage after death. Budge drew on papyri held in the British Museum, where he worked.

The weighing of the heart against a feather, the forty-two judges before whom the dead declare innocence, and the Field of Reeds promised to the justified all appear. Budge's renderings have been corrected by later Egyptology, yet his edition carried these texts to a wide public for the first time and still reads powerfully.
tob-13338:
Paramahansa Yogananda published his Autobiography of a Yogi in 1946, and the memoir did more than any other single book to bring yoga to America. Yogananda tells of his Bengali childhood, his search for a master, and his meeting with his guru, Sri Yukteswar. Training, travel, and teaching in India fill the first half.

Encounters with saints, reports of miracles, and conversations with figures such as Mahatma Gandhi give the narrative its wonder-tale quality. Yogananda then crosses to the United States, where he founded the Self-Realization Fellowship. Part spiritual autobiography and part introduction to Kriya Yoga, the book has guided millions of Western readers onto the path ever since.
tob-4138:
Paracelsus, the fiery Swiss physician born Theophrastus von Hohenheim, gets his English dress in Waite's translation of his hermetic and alchemical writings. Volume one covers the elements, the arcana of nature, and his attacks on the medicine of the schools. Paracelsus called himself the Luther of healing, and he wrote like it.

Disease, for him, has seeds and signatures that the wise physician reads in nature herself. Alchemy serves medicine, not gold-making greed. The prose erupts with scorn, prayer, and sudden insight. Verified from the 1919 edition, Waite's first volume gives the Renaissance rebel at full voice, in Victorian English.
treatises-on-physiology-and-phrenology-1: Treatises on Physiology and Phrenology, 1838. The twin treatises. This book preserves that work. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
un-ga-res-38:
Panama came to the young United Nations with a draft Declaration on the Rights and Duties of States. It was a bid to write down the basic rules of how states must treat each other. Resolution 38, passed on 11 December 1946, sets the draft on a long road of review. The Secretary-General must send the text at once to all member states and to bodies that work on world law.

Comments were due back by 1 June 1947. The draft then goes to a new Assembly team charged with the study of how world law should be codified. That team must report to the second regular session, and the question earns a place on that session's agenda.
un-ga-res-58-238:
Guatemala asked for one more year of the UN watch, and Resolution 58/238, passed in 2003, weighs the plea. The Verification Mission in Guatemala had its term stretched through 2003 by a vote of the year before. The state restated its pledge to put the peace deals into full force. The follow-up team's timetable for the work now ran through 2004.

The text takes note of the state's wish to keep the mission through the end of 2004. A new state team would take office in January 2004, and the mission's watch in that first year counts for much. Civic groups in the land, and the world at large, had voiced worry at parts of the peace that still lagged. The plea is taken up in that light.
un-ga-res-a-69-38:
Trust between states can be built in space as on earth, argues Resolution A/69/38, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The vote recalls a chain of texts since 2005 on trust-building steps in outer space. It also recalls a 1993 report of the Secretary-General, which held a study by state experts on how such steps could work above the earth.

All states hold the right to study and use space under world law, the text affirms. To bar an arms race in space serves peace for all, and it is a must for joint work in the peaceful use of space. Open word on space plans, shared by all, is the path the vote commends.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 38 was adopted on 11 December 1946, at the fifty-fifth plenary meeting. It set the draft Declaration on the Rights and Duties of States in motion. The Assembly told the Secretary-General to send the draft, put forward by Panama, at once to all member states. He was to send it also to bodies working on international law. He was to ask for their comments and views before 1 June 1947. He was to pass what came back to its new committee on writing down international law.

Resolution 58/238 of 23 December 2003 is the General Assembly's final Guatemala verification decision. It renews the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala for 2004. That was the last year of the agreed peace implementation timetable. The text reviews the mission's reports and the Secretary-General's account of the peace process.

For its closing phase the mission is told to concentrate on human rights. It is told to concentrate on demilitarization and strengthening civilian power. The Assembly voices concern at intimidation aimed at justice officials, human rights defenders, and journalists. It also welcomes an agreement for a United Nations human rights office to open in Guatemala in 2004. That way monitoring would continue after the mission itself wound down. The decision thus planned an orderly handover rather than an abrupt end to a decade of verification.

Resolution 69/38 of the General Assembly backs transparency and confidence-building measures in outer space work. The Assembly urges member states to review and apply the measures put forward by its Group of Governmental Experts in its 2013 report. They should do so by choice, through national mechanisms. It sends recommendations to the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space, the Disarmament Commission, and the Conference on Disarmament. It decides to convene a meeting of its First and Fourth Committees. The meeting is on challenges to space security and sustainability.
un-sc-res-1038: One of the Council's formal texts, Resolution 1038 is carried in this catalog under 1992. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1338:
East Timor's road to independence shaped a mandate renewal on 31 January 2001. The Secretary-General had reported on 16 January, and the goal was independence by the end of 2001. The United Nations Transitional Administration, UNTAET, was handing more power to East Timorese hands. Large numbers of refugees still sat in camps in West Timor, where militia activity threatened them.

The Council extended UNTAET's mandate to 31 January 2002. The special representative was told to keep delegating authority to the East Timorese people as a core part of the transition. Donors and financial bodies were called to fund the territory's needs, including the creation of an East Timor defence force. UNTAET had to answer the militia threat with robust action under resolution 1272 (1999). The Council also backed fixes to the justice system and a full solution to the refugee problem across the border.
un-sc-res-138:
Resolution 138, adopted on 23 June 1960, examines Argentina's complaint about Adolf Eichmann. Israeli agents had seized Eichmann, a former Nazi officer accused of mass crimes against the Jews, and taken him from Argentina to Israel to stand trial. Argentina said the transfer violated its sovereignty.

The Council agrees that violating a member state's sovereignty clashes with the Charter, and warns that repeats of such acts would breed insecurity and distrust. At the same time, it notes the worldwide condemnation of Nazi persecution and the wish that Eichmann face proper justice. It states plainly that the resolution must not be read as excusing the crimes he was accused of.
un-sc-res-1438: The catalog's entries for 2002 include Resolution 1438 of the United Nations Security Council. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1538:
Claims of corruption in Iraq's oil-for-food program reached the Council in 2004. News reports had questioned how the program was run. On 21 April 2004 the Council welcomed an independent high-level inquiry. The probe would study efforts by Iraq's former government to evade sanctions. Bribery, kickbacks, and surcharges on oil sales were named. So were illicit payments tied to humanitarian goods.

The Council calls on all states to cooperate fully with the inquiry. The Coalition Provisional Authority in Iraq had the same duty. National regulators were singled out as holders of key records. The Council said it looked forward to the final report. The inquiry's findings later confirmed large-scale abuse of the program.
un-sc-res-1638:
Liberia's former president faced arrest if he came home, under a 2005 ruling. Charles Taylor had left power in 2003 and taken shelter in Nigeria. He stood indicted by the Special Court for Sierra Leone. That court charged him over his role in Sierra Leone's civil war. On 11 November 2005 the Security Council added a task to its Liberia mission. The Council thanked Nigeria for helping to calm the region.

UNMIL troops gained the power to seize Taylor if he returned to Liberia. They would hold him and send him to Sierra Leone for trial. He did try to flee Nigeria months later and was caught. He was then sent to face the court. The mandate is a rare case of peacekeepers ordered to arrest a named man.
un-sc-res-1738:
War reporting gained formal protection in Resolution 1738, adopted in December 2006. Journalists were being killed and kidnapped in growing numbers in Iraq and other conflicts. The Council stated clearly that media workers in war zones count as civilians under the law of war.

The text condemns deliberate attacks on reporters, demands their release when seized, and reminds fighters that news equipment is not a military target. It also asks the Secretary-General to track the issue in his reporting. For readers, the resolution is the Security Council's clearest statement that silencing witnesses is itself a crime of war.
un-sc-res-1938:
Liberia's mission gained a further year by a decision of 15 September 2010. The Secretary-General's report of 11 August 2010 advised the renewal. Liberia's Truth and Reconciliation Commission had sent its final report. Progress on the drawdown benchmarks, above all the national police, was mixed, and violent crime stayed a real problem.

The Council let UNMIL help the Liberian government, as asked, with its 2011 polls for president and parliament. Help would cover transport, secure conditions, and joint work with the poll commission. Free, fair, and peaceful elections were made a core benchmark for the mission's drawdown. UNMIL and the government were told to press on with plans for handing security duties to Liberian authorities. The Secretary-General would send a technical team after the elections to set timelines for further troop cuts.
un-sc-res-2338: Kept under number 2338, a Security Council resolution survives in official-record form through English Wikisource. The number jumps ahead in the sequence preserved by this collection, into the Council's later output. The text at that address is complete: stated grounds, recalled precedents, and numbered decisions, kept together as the members issued them.
un-sc-res-238: Adopted by the Security Council and numbered 238, this formal text is catalogued under the year 1967. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-338:
The October war of 1973 had run for two weeks when the Council set its terms on 22 October. Israel was fighting Egypt and Syria. Resolution 338 is short, with only three points, but it became one of the Council's best-known texts. It was adopted that day, in the middle of the fighting.

All parties to the fighting had to cease all firing at once. All military activity had to end no later than twelve hours after the decision was adopted. The forces would stop in the positions they then held. Right after the cease-fire, the parties had to start carrying out Resolution 242 of 1967, in all its parts. Talks also had to start at the same time, under suitable auspices. Their aim was a just and lasting peace in the Middle East.
un-sc-res-38:
India and Pakistan faced the Council together for the first time in January 1948. The subject was Kashmir, disputed since the partition of British India. On 17 January 1948 the Council heard both governments. It noted the urgency of the situation. Days earlier its president had urged restraint on both sides, and both had pledged to honor the Charter.

The resolution calls on India and Pakistan to calm the situation at once. They should use every means they have, including appeals to their own people. They must avoid statements or acts that could make matters worse. Each government also had to tell the Council at once of any material change. The vote was nine to none, with two abstentions.
un-sc-res-738:
Security Council Resolution 738, adopted on January 29, 1992, recommended Tajikistan for membership in the United Nations. Tajikistan had declared independence from the Soviet Union in September 1991, weeks before the union itself came apart. The poorest of the new central Asian republics, it moved at once to claim a place in the world body.

The Assembly admitted Tajikistan on March 2, in the same wave as its neighbors. Within months the country slid into a civil war that lasted five years, which makes this calm formal vote read like the quiet before a storm. The short text still marks the legal start of Tajikistan's life as a sovereign state.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 1038, adopted on 15 January 1996, authorizes United Nations military observers to keep monitoring the demilitarization of the Prevlaka peninsula for a further three months. One more three-month extension is possible, if the Secretary-General reports it would continue to lower tension. Prevlaka, disputed between Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, had been demilitarized under a 1992 joint declaration. The Council also asks for a report by 15 March 1996. The report is on progress toward a peaceful settlement, and on whether another organization might take over the monitoring.

Resolution 1338, adopted unanimously on 31 January 2001, steers East Timor through its last year before independence. The UN transitional administration, UNTAET, was governing the territory after the violence of 1999. The Secretary-General's January report backed giving East Timorese a growing share in running their own affairs, with independence aimed for the end of 2001.

The Council extended UNTAET's mandate for another year, to January 2002. It urged further steps to hand authority to the East Timorese as an essential part of the transition, and backed plans for free and fair elections run with them. It also repeated a warning from its own visiting mission: strong international support would still be needed after independence day.

Argentina's complaint over the capture of Adolf Eichmann is the business of this text from 23 June 1960. Eichmann, accused of mass crimes against Jews under Nazi rule, had been taken from Argentina to Israel to face trial. Argentina argued the transfer violated its sovereignty as a member state.

The Council declared that acts harming a member state's sovereignty could endanger world peace if repeated. It asked Israel to make proper reparation under the Charter and the rules of international law. At the same time, it stressed that nothing in the text excused the crimes Eichmann was accused of, which the world condemned.

Bomb attacks in Bali, Indonesia, two days earlier are condemned on 14 October 2002. The blasts of 12 October killed and injured large numbers of people. Other recent terrorist attacks in various countries are cited in the same breath.

Deepest sympathy goes to Indonesia's government and people and to the victims and their families. All states are urged, under their duties in resolution 1373, to work urgently with the Indonesian authorities. The aim is to find and bring to justice those who carried out, organized, and sponsored the attacks. The Council also restates its resolve to fight terrorism in all its forms.

Serious corruption claims hung over the Iraq oil-for-food programme in 2004. Reports alleged bribes, kickbacks, and surcharges on oil deals. Saddam Hussein's government had gamed the system for years. Resolution 1538, adopted unanimously on 21 April 2004, backed a full investigation. The Secretary-General had already decided to launch one.

The Council welcomed the independent high-level inquiry. It called on Iraq, the Coalition Provisional Authority, and all states to cooperate fully. Regulators everywhere were asked to help. The text brands illegal acts by UN staff or contractors unacceptable. The inquiry, later led by Paul Volcker, became a landmark UN scandal probe. Its final report was awaited eagerly.

The label on this file names Iraq's war. The text is pure Liberia. Charles Taylor, the past Liberian strongman, sat in exile in Nigeria. A war crimes court in Sierra Leone had charged him. His crimes were said to span both lands' wars. Word spread that he might slip home. Resolution 1638 passed on 11 November 2005.

A new task was glued to the UN force in Liberia. If Taylor set foot in the land, UN troops had to seize and hold him. They would hand him to Sierra Leone for trial. The Liberian and Sierra Leonean states, and the Council, had to be kept in the loop. Praise went to Nigeria for sheltering him for a time, with world backing. His homecoming was ruled a threat to peace in the whole area.

Attacks on journalists and other media workers in armed conflict are condemned on 23 December 2006. Reporters were being killed, wounded, and kidnapped in war zones in rising numbers. Journalists on dangerous professional missions count as civilians under the Geneva Conventions, the Council recalls, and must be protected as such.

All parties to armed conflicts are demanded to stop deliberate attacks on journalists, media staff, and their equipment, and to end the culture of impunity for such acts. States are reminded of their duty to prosecute those responsible for grave breaches of humanitarian law against civilians, including media workers. The safety of journalists will also be addressed when peacekeeping mandates are set up and renewed.

Resolution 1938, passed on 15 September 2010, keeps the UN force in Liberia for one more year. A UN report of August 2010 urged the move. The Council cheered Liberia's work on mending its wounds and on growth. It praised steps against graft and for state grip on mines, farms, and woods. It also noted the truth panel's final report. That report gave Liberians a chance to talk through the roots of their war.

The force, UNMIL, won a new term to September 2011. Its drawdown was to be judged by set marks, most of all the growth of Liberia's own police. Some marks had been met. Others lagged. A UN team was to help plan the next cuts.

Resolution 2038, adopted on 29 February 2012, staffs the court that will inherit the Rwanda tribunal's unfinished business. The International Residual Mechanism was created in 2010 to take over from the war crimes tribunals for Rwanda and Yugoslavia as they closed. Its Rwanda branch was due to start work on 1 July 2012, and it needed a prosecutor.

The Council appointed Hassan Bubacar Jallow to the job, effective 1 March 2012, for a four-year term. Jallow was already prosecutor of the Rwanda tribunal, and the rules allowed him to hold both posts at once. The appointment kept one hand on the tiller as fugitive cases and archives passed to the successor court.

Cyprus is the subject of Resolution 2338, adopted on 26 January 2017. Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot leaders were negotiating a full settlement to reunite the divided island. Cyprus's government agreed that UNFICYP, the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, should stay beyond the end of January.

The Council extended UNFICYP's mandate until 31 July 2017. It welcomed the progress in the talks between the two leaders. Both sides were urged to seize the moment and secure a complete settlement. The text pressed for steps that build trust. More crossing points on the Green Line and renewed mine clearing in the buffer zone were named. The Committee on Missing Persons was also to get fuller access to its work.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force received another extension on 19 June 1967, when the Council adopted Resolution 238 unanimously. A report from the Secretary-General said the force was still needed to keep the peace on the island. The government of Cyprus agreed that it should stay beyond 26 June.

The Council reaffirmed its line of Cyprus resolutions reaching back to Resolution 186 of 1964. It urged the parties to show the utmost restraint. They were also asked to keep working together toward the Council's aims. The force's stay was extended for six months, ending on 26 December 1967. The Council expected that enough progress toward a solution would be made by then. That progress might let the force withdraw or shrink.

In the middle of the Yom Kippur War, the Council ordered the guns to stop. On 22 October 1973, it adopted Resolution 338. Egypt and Syria had attacked Israel just over two weeks before. Fighting still raged on two fronts when the Council met.

The text calls on all parties to cease fire at once. All military action must end within twelve hours. The sides must hold the ground they then stood on. Next, they must carry out Resolution 242, the land-for-peace formula of 1967. Talks toward a just and lasting peace must start at the same time. Those paired demands framed Middle East diplomacy for decades.

Kashmir's first winter of war drew the Council's opening plea in 1948. On 17 January, it adopted Resolution 38. Nine members voted yes and none voted no. The Ukrainian and Soviet republics held back. India and Pakistan had been free states for five months. Both were fighting over the princely state of Kashmir. Both had told the Council they meant to honor the UN Charter.

The text calls on both governments to act at once. All steps in their power must be used to calm the crisis. Public appeals to their own peoples are named as one such step. No words or acts may make things worse. Any big change must be reported to the Council straight away.

Tajikistan took its seat on the edge of civil war in 1992. On 29 January, the Council adopted Resolution 738 without a vote. The same round of meetings handled Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan. The Republic of Tajikistan had claimed freedom the September before. The Soviet Union was then in its last weeks. Tajikistan was the poorest of the Central Asian republics.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Tajikistan. Admission followed in March 1992. War broke out at home within months of the vote. The new state's first UN years were spent asking for aid. The seat it won here became its lifeline to the world.
